NEW YEAR WISHES. May the year now begun Be a prosperous one To you, and to those you hold dear! And blest be all they Who bless you this day And wish you a Happy New Year!

Over ills that are past May a thick veil be cast; May all that was dismal and drear Seem now but a shade By Providence made 're show forth a Happy New Year May your faith in the Friend Who will love to the end, Who hallow'd the groan and the tear— Your sorrow soon soothe, Your rough paths make smooth, Ind herald a Happy New Year!
- What you wish may you gain, May the hope be not vain That, henceforth, to you may appear The day you got this Was door-way to bliss Of many a Happy New Year! EDWARD N. MARKS.

THE SCREEN IN THE LUMBER ROOM. Yes, here it is, behind the box, That puzzle wrought so neatly— That paradise of paradox— We once knew so completely; You see it? 'Tis the same, I swear, Which stood, that chill September, Beside your Aunt Lavinia's chair, The year when . . . You remembev? Look, Laura, look! you must recall This florid" Fairies' Bower," This wonderful Swiss Waterfall, And this old " Leaning Tower ;" And here's the "Maiden of Cashmere," And here is Bewick's Starling; And here's the dandy Cuirassier You thought was—" such a Darling!" Your poor, dear Aunt! you knew her way; She used to say this figure Reminded her of Count D'Orsay "In all his youthful vigour ;" And here's the "cot beside the hill" We chose for habitation The day that . . . . But I doubt if still You'd like the situation ! Too damp—by far. She little knew, Your guileless Aunt Lavinia, Those evenings when she slumbered through "The Prince of Abyssinia." • That there were two beside her chair, Who both had quite decided To see things in a rosier air Than Rakselas provided! Ah ! men wore stocks in Britain's land, And maids short waists and tippets, When this old-fashioned screen was planned From hoarded scraps and snippets; But more—far more, I think, to me, Than those who first designed it, s Is this—in Eighteen-Seventy-Three I kissed you first behind ft! —Magazine of Art.

There is nothing formidable about death but the cousequences of it, and these we ourselves can regulate and control. " No, sir," was the prompt reply, "I am waiting for a gentleman !" As ships meet at sea, a moment together, when words of greeting ° must be spoken, and then away into the deep, so men meet in this world; and I think we should cross no man's path without hailing him, and, if he needs, giving him supplies.—Henry Ward Beecher. Stars shine brightest in the darkest night: torches are better for beating; grapes come not to the press; spices smell the best when they are bruised; young trees root faster for shaking; gold looks brighter for scouring ; juniper smells sweetest in the fire; the palm tree proves' the better for pressing; camomile, the more you tread it ' the more you spread it How often is it difficult to be wisely charitable; to do good without multiplying the sources of evil. To give alias is nothing unless you give thought also. It is written not "blessed is he that feedeth the poor," but '4 blessed is he that considereth the poor." A little thought and a little kindness are often worth more than a great deal of money. There are two kinds of girls; one is the kind,that ap- pears best abroad, the girls that are good for parties, ' rides, visits, balls, &c., and whose chief delight is in all such things. The other is a kind which appears best at home, the girls thatare useful and cheerful in the dining room, the sick room, and all the precincts of home. They differ widely in character. One is frequently a torment at home; the other is a blessing. One is a moth, con- suming everything about her; the other is a sunbeam, inspiring life and gladness all along the pathway.= Onward. CHILDHOOD'S BURDENS.—In nine cases out of ten a man's life will not be a success if he does not bear bur- dens in childhood. If the fondness or vanity of father or mother has kept him from hard work, if another has always helped him out at the end of his squabble, if what was light always fell to him, arid what. was heavy to someone else, if he has been permitted to shirk until shirking has become a habit, his life will be a failure. On the other hand, if a boy has been brought up to do his part, never allowed to shirk legitimate responsibility or dodge work, whether or not it made his head ache or soiled his hands, until bearing burdens has become a matter of pride, the heavy end of the wood his choice, the blements of success are his, and at some time, in some way, the world will recognise his capacity. He had been going to see her a long time, but had not stated the object of his visits, and she was desirous of knowing something of the future. The last night he called he seemed to be quite sad, and after several well. developed sighs he said, "Life is full—very full of bitter- ness, isn't it ?" "Oh, I don't know !" she responded cheerfully; "I haven't much cause to complain." " Possibly not now, Mary; but the bitter cup has been placed to your lips." "Yes, Henry; my parents are I dead." "And is there no bitterness in that, Mary? Is it not very, very sad to be an orphan?" "Of course it is, Henry; but you see "—and she blushed—" it relieves you of the embarrassment to ask father." ARITHMETICAL VATICINATIONS.—Some years before 1369—but Ido not remember exactly when—a table was circulated to prove that, by adding the dates of the Em- peror's birth, that of the Empress, and that of their marriage, to the year 1852, when Napoleon was made Emperor, the result would give the year in which either he would die or resign; and it is worthy of remark that the year 1869 thus obtained is the year when Napoleon 111. abdicated personal government and prepared his downfall in 1870. Nor is it less singular that the same process applied to Louis Philippe gave the year 1848, that in which he abdicated. Dickens and Landseer—the author and artist—were dining together, when a servant entered and calmly in- quired, "If you please, Sir Edwin, did you order a lion?" The horror of Dickens may be imagined--the gardens of the Zoological Society not being far distant; but it was no live lion that the servant was inquiring about. One of these noble animals had recently died at the gardens, and the menagerie authorities wished to know whether Sir Edwin wished—as he frequently did—to sketch the carcase before it was buried. THE FOUNDATION OF SUCCESS.—" Untie the strings," said a ynost successful merchant to a lad who was open- ing a parcel. "Young man, untie the strings; do not cut them." It was the first remark that he had made to a new employe. It was the first lesson the lad had to learn, and it involved the principle of success or failure in his business career. Pointing to a well dressed man behind the counter, the merchant said, "There is a man who always whips out his scissors and cutwthe string of • the packages in three or four places. He is a good sales- man, but he will never be anything more. I presume he lives from hand to mouth, and is more or less in debt. The trouble. with him is that he was never taught to save. I told the boy just now to untie the string, not so much for the value of the string as to teach him that everything is to be saved and nothing, wasted. If the idea can be firmly impressed upon the mind of a be- ginner in life that nothing was made to be wasted, that things the most trivial have their uses, you have laid the foundation of success" EDUCATION.—HuxIey had well asked "whether, if it were perfectly certain that the life and fortune of every one of us would one day depend on our winning a game of chess, we should not all learn something of the game? Yet it is a very plain truth that the life and fortune of every one of us depend on our knowing something of the rules of a game infinitely more difficult. It is a game which has been played for untold ages—every man and woman of us being one of the two players. The chessboard is the world, the pieces are the phenomena of the universe, the rules of the game are what we call the o laws of nature. The player n the other side is hidden from us. We know that his play is always fair, just, and patient. But also we know, to our cost, that he never overlooks a mistake, or makes the smallest allowance for ignorance. To the man who plays well the highest stakes are paid with overflowing generosity, but one who plays ill is checkmated—without haste, but without re- morse."—Quoted by Sir J. Lubbock at Birmingham. The most carefully edited journal is fallible. In The Times office, it is said, proof-readers are fined for every blunder that eludes them. On the New York Herald they have been suspended for weeks. In spite of this severe discipline the Herald once made the astonishing an- nouncement that a long line of scorpions' feathers filed into the church,' instead of surpliced fathers.' A re- porter on that paper had occasion to quote a verse from a familiar hymn in which the word "herald" occurred. The proof-reader dutifully underscored the word, and the verse appeared: " Hark ! The Herald angels sing." It was in the World's report of a political meeting that the word "shouts" was so ludicrously misprinted as to make the blunder famous. "The snouts of ten thousand Democrats rent the air," read the report. A few years ago the journalist, who is widely known as " Gath," wrote a Fourth of July article. With fervid eloquence he told how the effete monarchs of the old world trembled in their boots when they read the immortal words penned by Thomas Jefferson. "Thrones reeled," wrote the impassioned Gath. Next morning he saw in type :—" Thomas reeled." The story is told that Ernest Ronan once had occasion to telegraph across the British Channel the subject of a proposed lecture of his in West- minster Abbey. The subject as written by him was "The Influence of Rome on the Formation of Chris- tianity." It was published in England as'" The Influ- ence of Rum °Who Digestion of Humanity.," THE WISE AND THE Fooeisn iNionsit—One night two hungry mice entered a pantry, and, to their great de- light, found a large piece of cheese. "If there is one thing I like more than another it is cheese," whispered one. "Just so," mumbled the other; and they began to make up for their long fast. After they had been nib- bling some time, one of them drew back as though satis- fied. "What !" exclaimed his companion, "you are not going yet,l hope? Why, this is the best feast we have had for many a night." "I admit that," replied the other. "The cheese is certainly very nice, but you must remember that in coming here we entered through a very small hole indeed, and if we should eat too freely we shall not be able to pass back in case a cat should pop in upon us." Nonsense," squeaked the other; "I never saw such a mouse as you are. When I find anything good to eat I always make the most of it, and take ray chances." So he nibbled at the cheese again, while the wise mouse looked on, fearing for the safety of his friend. A pussy that had been watching their move- ments for some time now pounced in without knocking, and of course there was a hasty scampering for the hole on the part of the mice. The wise mouse, who had eaten moderately, reached the hole first, and escaped without any difficulty. The silly mouse, however, who had eaten without any regard for the future, was rather slow in getting to the hole, and even after he rehched it was too full to squeeze through, but stuck fast until two great paws were upon him, and before long he was de- livered over to the tender care of a whole family of kit- tens, who were soon crying out, "Oh ! mamma, get us more mouse. It is so nice." "Dear me !" said the wise mouse a few minutes afterwards, poking up his head to seek for his friend. "Dear me! What a great moral lesson has been illustrated to-night !" ELECTRIC HO! SE BELLS.

. . the -turf has been cut down to the level of its de- posit the underlying land is brought into cultiva- tion as agricultural land. The fact of the general use of the moss litter as bedding for live stocks, would seem to open out a profitable basis for British enterprise. From what we have seen of the Continental article now in use, it appears to be identical with the turf from our own mosses, partially dried, and broken up fine. In the potting of plants, this turf is used in admixture with other moulds by gardeners, and this fact would indicate that when the moss litter is saturated with the urine from the animals, and mixed with the dung, it will prove a valuable manure for the growth of agricultural crops. It is to be regretted that our railway companies should continue to give prefer ential rates to all foreign pro- ' ducts, whilst heavily handicapping British productions, and it is quite possible that the foreigners owe their monopoly of moss litter to this cause. We venture to think, however, that the article, not- withstanding the action of railway companies; would prove a remunerative British industry, for the native producers would have four counteracting influences over the single adverse one of higher railway carriage. First, the lesser mileage to markets; second, the utilisation of a product which is now lying as waste and unprofitable, useless to the owners of the land, useless to the tenants of the land; third, the bringing into cultivation of large acreages of land for the production of agricultural crops, and thus enlarging the area of the cultivated lands of the United Kingdom, whilst adding to the value and scope of our manurial products; fourth, in many of the districts where the peat mosses exist there are seaports adjacent, and the finished product might be despatched independent of prohibitive railway tariffs. At a time when so much British capital is lying idle, awaiting profitable investment, it appears to the writer that the establishment of companies to work the peat mosses of the United Kingdom, looking to the extent of the foreign imports, would prove safe and remunerative, for there can be no doubt but that the owners of such would give easy terms in order to have the land stripped of its covering of turf, and left in a position for easy • conversion into agricultural land. Such an industry . ' would also afford employment to men at a time when so many men are idle through general trade depression, and agricultural depression. Although not practically acquainted with much of the . route that the Thirlmere waterway will take, the writer is under the impression that a considerable area of pfeat moss will be found in the cutting, and its conversion into moss litter for bedding might be made a profitable industry by the Manchester Corporation.' .

, knew the soldiers would be on the Ina-arch. Then the sun went down, and the grey mist from the river spread over the moor, and up the glen of Moy. When she got to yon pate I showed you between the hills,-; her head was dizzy, and her heart went jumping lip into her mouth, but she ran on, till Gillian, the piper, who was shutting up the castle gate, saw her coming, and called to her aunt, 'Come here, Mistress Flora, and see if it is not Annot Fraser coming run- ning like a mad hare up the glen." " 'Sure enough it is:Annot. Gin she have gone mad? She looks as if she had seen a wraith! "They went to meet her, and Annot fell quite f dead-like at their feet. Gillian carried her into May Hall, and Mis- tress Flora get some of the lady's strong waters for her. When she came out of the faint she gasped 'The prince! The English!' ' a The lady came to see what it was all about; and soon Annot was able to tell that the English soldiers were coming to seize the prince, and how she had run for ten miles before them to give the lady warning. They were all frightened when they heard the evil tidings, and Gillian said, 'We must get the prince out by the postern gate that opens up the glen, and Jan, the gillie, will guide him to the hut of Witch Moray; the Southerners will never find him there.' "'No, Gillian,' said the lady, 'his highness is weary even unto death; he lies in a deep sleep on the state-chamber bed. I cannot send him out with none but Jan; we must hold the castle. You must man the pass, and keep the base Southerners from the gate.' .4 'Man the pan!' said Gillian. 'Does my lady know that there are but three men of us, old Dugald the blacksmith, young Jan, and me ?' Call them here,' said the lady. When they, came in, looking feared enough, she ordered, 'Go, Dugald, beat on your anvil, and clang as loud tie if all the claymores of the clan were being beaten and sharpened for a foray. You, bal, will.march down the glen, shouting out our battle-cry, as if all the clan were behind you ready to dash down the foe. Gillian, you must take the bagpipe and play the pibroch of Macintosh as if you were leading your chief to victory.' "The soldiers did not know the short ways across the moor like Annot; then they lost time seeking the ford, and the lady was ready for them when the sound of marching feet was heard by Sheila Boyd, the still-room maid, who had been sent to the tower to listen, for the people said she had ears like the fairies, she could hear thelgrass growing. When the „soldiers got fairly into the glen, they were quite dazed by a noise like the clanging of swords in the distance. Then the pihroch of Chattan came shrieking down the pass like the cry of a Highland eagle, and still nearer came the shout of a strong young voice making the rocks ring with the cry of Macintosh. The captain, turning to his men, said, 'My lads, these wily Highlanders have thought to catch us in a trap, we are betrayed into the hands of Macintosh. From that devilish noise, too, you hear:the clan there! Likely it is a lie, too, about the Young Pretender being here. Retreat before the Highland devils dash down on us. See, tbe signal on tower and the lights from the win- dows of Moy! "With that they all turned round and stumbled down the pass, but when they came to the river they missed the ford, in the dark, and thirty men of them were carried down by the current and drowned. "After all was safe, the lady came to where Annot was lying, all her clothes wet with the sweat of her running, even her hair, which had fallen loose over her shoulders, as wet as if she had been dragged through the river. 'Flora,' she called, 'see to this brave girl; take off her damp clothes and lay her in a warm bed. God grant she may not suffer for her loyalty to her prince, and her kind thought for her lover's oleo.' Then the great lady kissed Annot, and said, 'The Macintosh will reward you, my brave ehild ! ' " Prince Charlie was so used to the noise of camps that he slept through all the stir, and knew nothing of his danger till the morning. Throtigh the night the Gillie went to In- verness for help, and brought back with him a band of the Clan Cameron to guard the prince on the road. When the lady told Prince Cerullo of the girl who had run ten miles before the soldiers to give the warning at Moy, he called for Annot and kissed her cheek, which was as white as a ghost's, after her faintness from running. " Ala, Lady Meointoeh! how sad that I have no token of gratitude to give her; bat when I get my own again I shall think of Annot! "The lady answered, 'lf your Royal litighness will con- demand to give her a lock of your own hair, I am sure she will care for that more than gold.' "The prince drew his sword, aad cut off a curio! his yellow hair, and gave it to Annot. She went on her knees te take it, and kissed his royal hand.' "You will know from the history books how Prince Charlie and his Highlanders were beaten by the English soldiers on the moor of Culloden, how he had to hide like a hunted fox among the; glens and rocks. At last he got a ship to carry him away to Fusee, far from the bonny Highlands." "Yes, Marv, I know his sad end, but what became of brave Annot i'" "Oh, the lady kept her safe at Moy till she was wedded to Hanish, and, you see, he was my great great grandfather. The Macintosh gave her this croft for a dowry, and Hamish was the proud man to have so brave a bride, and he called it " Annot's Croft,' for it was the reward for her race to save the prince, and the honour of her lover's clan." Donald got up stiffly, and growing the room, unlocked an oaken cupboard, and brought out a little silver box; opening it solemnly, he put it in my hands. There lay a little leek of yellow hair. ' "The lady put Prince Charlie's curl in that box and gave it to Annot when she wedded Hamish, my great great grandfather." "It is a beautiful story, Marra I thank you for telling It to me, for I have read nothing about it in all nay history books. Anton was a splendid girl, and some of her spirit has come down to you, I am sure." In telling the story of leer ancestors, which had become to her as part of her own life, Mary had lost her shyness, ler eyes were dilated with excitement, and her young face glowed with heroic fervour. ,1 Looking Into those beaming eyes, I said— " Sorely you could do as bravely as Anna, and suffer ' even death for one yon loved 2" I think I could," said Mary; and, coming to herself, ' she dropped her little head ia modest confusion. * * * * * Now I am in my studio in London working for the next exhibition; but the picture which interests my visitors most is one of a Highland interior, lit only by a glowing peat fire. An old man is seated on a high-backed chair, while a golden-haired girl on a low stool by his knee seems, from her eager gesture, to be telling a story to a matt who is almost hidden in the grey dimness of the chimney corner. A woman bends over a spinning-wheel, with the fire-glow reflected on her quaint high cap and solemn, dark eyes. My picture is called "A Highland Lassie's Story." If my fair maiden of ths North only brings me as much luck as my dark-eyed Italian Cermela did, I shall have good reason to thank pretty Mary Mclntosh for telling me her version of the "Rout of Moy."_ELIZSESITH WRIGHT, in the Christmas part of "The Girls' Own Paper."

NORTH-LANCASHIRE AGRICUI.TUELA.L NOTES.-The young wheat plant is picking up again after the severe frost, and looks green and healthy. As the land is yet too wet to go upon, the needs of live stock occupy chief atten- tion. When work is a little slack on the farm it would be well to have an 'overhaul of the imPlements and machinery of the farm, all of which are now apt to suffer from rust. A stitch in time of this kind fre- quently saves ninety-and-nine at hay and grain harvest, a little oil and paint saving the pocket very much, to say I nothing of the worry of having machinery breaking ' down just when most wanted. 'Last year one of my I neighbours purchased a Hampshire ram. The latter ' stood our seasons well, and, having been crossed with Leicester, Cheviot, and half-bred ewes, the result has been most satisfactory. This week some of his produce are in the Christmas market, and the butcher speaks highly of them. He says the Hampshire has not only given a heavier weight per quarter, but there is also a largerlroportion of lean meat to the fat.-R., in. Agri.. v.ltural Gaz-ette. -.1 POLITICS V. AGRICULTIYRE.-The other day I met a farmer friend leading his cart nag; it was raining cats and dogs, the frost having broken down. He said he was going to get sharped ; the wind was working round from the west to the north, and, if it kept up, it would freeze during the night, and he would be unable to get to town I with his milk cart unless he got the nag shamed. On; parting, he asked me how the elections were going, and also what party was now in power-the Liberal or the Conservative? We had just completed a very hot con- test, in which the ex-Solicitor-Gerieral, Sir Ferrer Herschell, had been defeated by a local ironmaster. The next morning the roads were one sheet of ice. Now here was a man, risen from the farm servant class, now farming his 200 acres and upwards, paying from £2 to £2 10s. per acre; a man who, throughout all his depres- sion, has continued to make his farm realise a profit; a man who had the prevision to get his nag sharped io a downpour of rain so as not to miss his next morning's milk market; and yet did not know which party hell the reins of government in the country !-R. AGRICULTURAL DEPRESSION IN KENT.-The agricultural depression in Kent is severely felt. Many workhouses have had the number of their inmates increased by one- half, and in some cases they are even doubled. The wages of agricultural labourers have been systematically reduced, and the business of the county courts is 13ecom- ing greatly augmented by claims which are undefended and unpaid simply because of the scarcity of money. ...Lea by a, wandered on for miles, till I came to a river with slender young birches en its banks, peeping over to gaze at their own pretty shadows in the brown mirror of water. Yee, it was: brown, but clear and bright, changing into amber where the sun's rays struck the water, broken by the jutting rocks ,which here ard there stemened the current. The lovely, lovely scene touched me by its pathetic beauty. I got out my box of water-colours and worked away for a long time without hearing a sound. Then, suddenly, that strange thrill passed through me which, like a magnetic touch, warns us that another human being is near. Looking up quickly I saw an old Highlander, dressed in homespun :blue, watching me curiously, with Preen, grey eyes. He said (in the wonder- fully fine English which struck me: in the Inverness peasants)— "I see you're painting our young birches,seir." "That's what I'm after; but, my good:friend, can you tell use of any place near where I can get something to eat? I have walked from Inverness, and I'm as hungry as a trooper."; "There's no inn within three miles, sir; but down in yon .hollow is my little house, where you're kindly: welcome to share our dinner." I needed no second invitation, and thanked him heartily, then off we set to the farm, or croft, as my guide called it. After a short walk we came in sight of a .long, low cottage, roofed with thatch, with a stock of "peat ''standing like a , dusky pyramid against the whitewashed gable. My host ushered me into the:kitchen. ,At one end was a large wide fireplace, over which a round ipot, with three little feet, hung from A steel bar. On the hearth stood a , woman, with a:sweet, motherly:face, crowned by a whitecap, with a stiff, tall back, lined with tartan ribbon. To her the matt introduced me, saying, "Elspeth, I met this gentleman ' drawing the bits of trees down by the river, and have brought him home4to get a bite with:us. But where's my IiABAI6, Mary ? " helcmtinned. "She'll be in this minute," said Elspeth, and as she spoke a young girl came in carrying a milk pail, and curtseyed shyly to the stranger. What;,a bonnie Scotch laseie she was! her yellow hair braided round a neat little head, from which shone, like twin stars, soft grey eyes full of the pathos which is never far to seek in the true Celtic type. A coarse but clean cloth was spread on the deal table, the three-legged pot was slung from the tire, from ira large dish was filled with mealey potatoes, laughing through their ragged coatis, and with a large flagon of new milk, and a hunch of home-made cheese. I made a dinner ;worthy of a hungry man. With the hospitality of the Highlands the good people asked no questions of theiv guest, but the old man told me that his 1,4111. was Donald Macintosh, and that he was a crofter on the Moy land. "Aid my name is Richard Somerset," I said. "I am an artist in London, and have come to the Highlaeds fir ,my health." Elspeth exclaimed, "I thought you looked bnt weakly, sir." "Well, I am not veryrstrong,l and j am tired with the morning's walk." ." Oh, sir, you won't be thinking of tramping that weary way back te the town again ?" "I fefkr I must, unless you can take me in for the night." " Indeseliwe can, if you will be pleased with a bed in our long room." " Pleased ! I am only too thankful to be allowed to stay. Is there any place where I can get a pretty sketch in the afternoon beyond your farm ?" Mary whispered, " The island, mother; that would make a bonny picture." "It would that, my dear; you can show the gentleman the road to it when you take the cows to the pasture." I was enjoying a rest and a smoke with Donald in the rustic porch, when three little cows came frisking round the corner from the byre, togging their horned heads, and sniffing up the perfumed air of the bean-field with wide-spread nostrils. Mary followed them, her little rosebud face hidden in the depths of a tunnel-shaped calico sun- bonnet. Catching up my sketch book I joined the little train, and in the wake of the cows trudged along a bleak road, which did not look promising for my sketch. But when we got round a corner, what was my surprise to find before me a scene really idyllic in its soft beauty. Below us lay a silvery lake, with a small green island, in which were the ruins of a Highland keep, shaded by the feathery plumes of the young larches. The brown wastes and the craggy hills around looked all the browner and barer in contrast with the verdant gem, which in so strange a Setting, lo•ked as if it had strayed from some sunnier region. "That is Moy Island," said Mary. "Once our chief's castle was there, but it was bunted down, long long ago." It is a lovely place, Mary, and the very thing for a pic- ture, as you thought. I shall sit down just here, where I can see the grey ruins and those pals blue hills, which look so far, far away over the brown moorlands. Will yea wait and tell me if the fairies live on Moy Island yet? for, sure I am, in the good old days they must have had many a merry dance on that soft greensward. "Oh, sir, father says tt is all nonsense about the fairies." "'Don't.you know any stories, Mary ?"I "Yes, I know one story of 'Moy Hall,' for, you see, it's all about my great, great grandmother. Do you see yon glen among the hills? In it is the castle of Clan Chattel:, called Moy Hall. Once bonnie Prince Charlie slept there, before the battle of Culloden." "I have seen Culloden Moor, Mary, and the green mounds among the heather where the grayee of the poor soldiers lie. But, come, tell me the story of your great, great grand- mother, and what she had to do with Moy Hall." "Oh, sir, I can't wait now, but if you will come to the kitchen at night after the cows are milked, then I'll tell it to you." When I got back to the croft I found a grand tea ready for me • piles of scones, thin as a wafer, which melted like honey in my mouth; a splendid trout, fresh from the river, cooked te a turn, and a jug of rich, yellow cream flanking the big brown teapot. Hind Elspeth had catered well for . me. In the waning light I wandered down by the river till Donald came to ask me to join them in the kitchen. I found Elspeth at her spinning wheel, and Mary by the flickering firelight knitting a long blue stocking for her father. What a subject it would have made for Schalcken! Little flames spurting out and lighting up the dresser at the at end with its racks of crockery, then dying back to the centre glow, only to spring out on the other side and reveal in a little patch of light, with a frame of undefined gloom, old Donald seated on a high-backed chair, his little daughter close to him, her steel needles reflecting the broken lights as the nimble fingers plied through them the meshes of the blue worsted. Donald lit his pipe with a glowing ember, and begged of me to do the same. I looked hesitatingly to ELspeth, but she said— "Never think of us, sir, we don't object to smoking like the town ladies; we are used to Donald's pipe, and if Evan Mohr (that's the keeper from Moy Hall) comes to see us of an evening, he smokes, too." "Speaking of Moy Hall reminds me that Mary pronriaed to tell me a story about it." Mary hung her head and blushed, saying, "Father will tell it better. "No, no, dearie," said Elspeth, " many's the time you've heard grandmother tell it, you might.have it by. heart; let father get his pipe in peace." Mary thus encouraged began in'a low, timid voice:— "You'll havelheard all about the '45, when bonnie Prince Charlie landed at Moidart and met the Highland chiefs in Glen Finnan. They rushed down on the Lowlands, and took Edinburgh, and the Prince lived in the old palace of Holyrood. Then he thought he would go right on to London, where King George was sitting on the throne, and get his golden crown for himself; and they went south to the town of Derby, but there the chiefs began to quarrel among themselves, some wanting to turn back, others to go on and poor Prince Charlie saw the beat way was to go back to Scotland. Very soon Ring George' sent his son with a great many soldiers to fight against Prince Charlie, and to kill him or bring him a prisoner to LLondon town. Inverness was held by the Highlanders,: and one day the Prince came from the castle there, to Moy Zell, with Cameron of Lochiel, to take counsel with The Macintosh,' who was setting out with the Clan Chattan that very day to waylay the English soldiers. Only three men were left with Lady Macintosh, but she had no fear. Before that lady was married to the chief of Clan: Chattan, she was a Misp Fraser of Lovat.'42Bhe got her schooling at a convent In Paris, and she used to go to the :court of King James, and once, at a ball, she danced a Highland reel :with the king's own son, the Father of Prince Charlie ; 'and the French king was there, and clapped his hands to see them dance it so finely! " This made her think all the more of Prince Charlie, and when she saw him look white and weary,'she said to The Macintosh," Let Prince:Charlie ,rest herethis night in peace." Lochiel said, You have:no guard, my lady. If Duncan Forbes should hear that his Royal Highness is in Moy and the Clan Chattan gone, he will eend;poldiers to seize the Prince.' Duncan Forbes is in Edinburgh,' sair:the lady, 'and there are no traitors in ClaniChattan ; 'Cumberland's men will never know that his highness is:here.' Prince Charlie told Lochiel to ride back to Inverness, and say he would be there in time for the council in the morning, for he would rest at Moy that night, as good old Lady Macintosh wished. "How King George's soldiers :heard, about it was never. found Out; perhaps there was a traitor among the Macin- toshes. Any way, news of it came to Lord Loudon's band, which had got to a clachan on the way north, ten miles from Moy. The officers were to sleep in the inn called the Lovat Arms.' "The who waited on them was Annot Fraser, and she was my great, great grandmother; her aunt was waiting woman to Lady Macintosh, and Annot was troth plighted with Harnish, the chief's henchman. Annot was making a bed in a little room, only divided from the parlour

When Milton was blind he married a shrew. The Duke of Buckingham called her a rose. "I'm no judge of colour," said Milton, "but it may be so, for I feel the thorns daily." The best thing to give to an enemy is forgiveness; to an opponent tolerance; to a friend your heart; to your child a good example; to a father deference; to a mother conduct that will make her proud of you; to yourself respect; to all men that charity which suffereth long and is kind. The virtue which the world wants is a healthful virtue, not a valetudinarian virtue; a virtue which can expose itself to the risks inseparable from all the spirited exer- tion, not a virtue which keeps out of the common air for fear of infection, and eschews the common food as too stimulating.

A HUNT STOPPED BY A PrassT.—The hunt of the county Limerick hounds was stopped on Monday at Rockhill, near Bruree, by the Rev. Mr. Sheehy, parish priest, and a crowd of peasantry. Mr. John Gubbins is .the master, and the Rev. Mr. Sheehy interviewed him with regard to his rela- tions with his tenantry. It appeared that Mr. Gubbins had offered his tenants an abatement of 25 per cent., but as he refused to make it a permanent settlement they declined to accept the terms. Father Sheehy suggested that the dis- pute should be referred to arbitration, and Mr. Gubbins, ,faiLing to fall in 'with his views, he threatened that hunting ' would be stopped. The crowd who accompanied the clergy- man cheered him, and it was evident from their attitude that they meant violence if the hunt should be persevered in. Mr. Gubbins, however, drew off the hounds and returned home.

THE RISING IN THE sOUDAN. DESPATCH FROM GEN. `STISPHENSON.--CAPTURE OF REBFale .NUGGARS. The following has been received from the War Office : From Lieut.-Gen. Sir F. Stephenson to Secretary of State for War.—Abri, January 2, 3-15 p.m. Butler at Erawe, 20 Miles south of here. Reports enemy's loss much heavier than at first supposed in our estimate as 600 killed. Enemy flying through Kuibar to Dongola." ABRI, SATURDAY.—The cavalry is now in pursuit of the enemy. The enemy lost 24 emirs and at least 600 men killed and wounded in Wednesday's engagements. Besides thase many of the Arabs died by the river side during the retreat. Among the enemy it was reported that 6,000 Turks and English were marching across the desert to Absarab, and they have tied direct to Dongola without stopping any- where. The villagers have been stripped by the enemy of their property. The Arabs have no reserve north of Berber. The health of the troops is good. The enemy have made no secret of their rout, and many fled by way of the West d.esert, expecting to be cut off at Absarab by our cavalry. le great quantity of correspondence has been fonnd which 'Will throw valuable light on the Arab movement. The 'nemy own that they were taken completely by surprise. Ike prisoners report that diseensions preYaß among the Kordofan and Darfour tribes. °Lino, Morinex.---eneral Grenfell telegraphs that on Saturday the stern-wheel steamer Lotus moved up the Nile to Absarat, thirty miles south of Abri, the ,present British adquarters, and ascertained that Mafid, with a few fol- lowers, was at Dulgo. The mounted men have returned Sayed Efferadi. The Lotus overtook and captured 'nine naggers, laden with arms, ammunition, and clothing. I Marry prisoners were also taken. The men in the nuggars -1,(1 at the approach of the Lotus, and the villagers also beat a hasty retreat. Dervishes were -seen all along the , Nile. Anal, hecarnay.—Oza hundred and fifty cavalry and Mounted infantry of the Camel Corps, under Capt. Smith- Dorrien, pursued the enemy to Absarat. The enemy had eftaPed over the left bank of the river. Among the docu- ments found at Maaatl's house was a complete muster roll of 10,000 men, who formed his advanced guard. Clothing and equipment lists were also found. The enemy's organi- setion appears to &Free been most complete. In their retreat the enemy left the Nile at Koyek, and proceeded by the desert to Dulgo, near Abu Fatmeh. Tnere they rallied, in Order to march to Abu Fatmeh, where Mahomed Elkheia Was encamped. THE TURKISH MISSION TO EGYPT. Cousraarriteomn„ TUESDAl.—Muktitar Pasha has sent a report to the Turkish Government, in whoa he describes the *cation in Egypt as unfavourable. THE TURKISH MILITARY PREPARATIONS. .30ersreterrirropaa, WEDNEYDAY.—It is stated that the Powers are in favour of the Forte's first making a proposal for the solution of the Roumelian crisis, which could sub- sequently be submitted for their discussion. It is generally believed in political circles that Russia is rapidly gaining Power in Constantinople. The Turkish military preparations continue, and a f ter- 'tiler batch of 40.000 redifs is expected from Syria. Part ,of 'these will be stationed on the Montenegrin frontier, where .considerable agitation prreails. ENGLAND AND BURAIAH. CALLA, MONDA.Y.—In the Legisletive Council to day the Viceroy alluded to Barmah. He said the arraneement under the proclamation was required by the actual circum- -stances of the moment, and would be shortly replaced by more elaborate machinery. The natare of this in all proba- bility would not be detertilined until he himself had visited Mandalay, and could submit a report on the condition of the country to the British Government. The following telegram from the Chief Commissioner has been received at the India Office :—Mandalav, Monday.— 'Prendergast reached Bhaneo. Cordially received by Bur- mese officials, %ciao had kept place quiet ' • also by Chinese merchants. No opposition on river. Prendergast leaves garrison at Bhamo. INDIA.—NEW TAXATION. CALCUTTA, MONDAY.—At to-day's sitting of the Legisla- tive Council Sir A. Colyiu, the Finance Minister, announced the introduction of a bill providing for the imposition of an incdme-tax of 2 per cent., or rather the erctension of the Present license tax to the incomes of professional men and officials, who have hitherto been exempt. Sir Auckland ex- plained that the new law would not extend to incomes under 500 rupees. The Viceroy accepted the responsibility of the measure. In his view, financial justice demanded the im- Position of an income-tax, and moreover no other course was open. The Government would only resort to an increase of the salt-tax in an extreme emergency. The deficit, which amounted to £2,000,000, was caused by the preparations due to the Russian scare, the depreciation of silver, the expendi- ture on the Bolan Railway, and the expedition to Burmah. The Viceroy further stated that with regard to Burmah the future system of government could not be developed until he had personally visited the country. The Mahara- jah of Cashmere has arrived here on a short visit to the 'Viceroy.

THE ANNEXATION OF BILKMAH.. A CLAIMANT FOR THE THRONE. An Ailahabad correspondent says :—Lord Doffarin, who is now quite recovered from the fever he contracted during his recent tour, will proceed to Burmah on the 2Eth of the

present month. The Daily Chronicle publishes the following, daced ;Ran- goon, Wednesday :—The pacification of Upper Burmah is not proceeding as rapidly as had been hoped and expected. In many parts of the country, and particularly in the neighbourhood of Mandalay, dacoity is rife, leading to troublesome and harassing skirmishes daily. The Alorripra Prince has mustered a very large force in the Paleik district near 'Mandalay, and is causing considerable trouble in con- sequence. He claims to succeed Thebaw as Sing of'Upper Burmah, and he said—as is very like!q, considering the force at his disposal —toP be supported in his claims by the people. Meanwhile he is, besides being a source of anxiety to the British expedition, collecting taxes from the people

states that at the end of December a band of rebels attacked and completely destroyed the Catholic mission station situated in the, mountainous district of Nghean, in the pro- vince of Annam killing a French missionary and between four and five hundred native Christians. General de Courcy adds that a column had been despatched in pursuit of the rebels, and had completely routed them, captutiug their arms and ammunition. TILE CAROLINE ISLANDS QUESTION. MADRID, MONDAY.—Senor Moret, Minister for Foreign Affairs, this afternoon presented the protocol relating to the settlement of the Caroline Islands question to the Cortes. Toe protocol, which consists of six articles, states that Germany recognises the priority of the Spanish occu- pation, and her sovereignty over the Caroline and Pellew groups. Spain, in return, grants to German subjects liberty of cqmmerce and navigation on the same terms as provided by the Sooloo protocol, together with the right to establish commerce and agriculture. Germany is also empowered to establish a naval coaling station. England claims the -same advantages. THE CHOLERA IN SPAIN. • MADRID, MONDAY.—Despite the extremely cold weather, the cholera epidemic is slowly extending, and this is caus- ing much anxiety. Five provinzes are already invaded— Huelva, Cadiz, Malaga, Granada. and Salamanca. At Al- geciras, on the opposite side of the bay to Gibraltar, Aga- monte,, Marbella, and Vitigudino the plague is unusually severe. At Marabella, a small port in Malaga. with a popu- lation of about 7,000 persons, the epidemic pas caused as many as 14 deaths in one day. GREAT FIRE AT DETROIT, DETROIT (Micnietaaa), SATURDAY.—The seed warehouses of Messrs. Ferry and Co., White's Theatre, and other build- ings here have been destroyed by fire. The loss is estima- ted at over 1,000,000 dellars.

SAME! WANDERS V. BOSTOCK STAR. These kaMIS met on the ground of the former, the game resulting in a win for the Wanderers by one goal, one try, 15 minor peints to nil. Sr. HELENS RECREATION V. SUTTON.—These clubs met on Saturday on the ground of the latter, a fast and pleasant game ending in a draw in favour of the Recreation by five minor points to four. NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS V. LOWER CRUMPSALL.—PIayed on Saturday on the ground of the former, the result being— Newton, one goal (from a disputed try) and two minor points; Cranapsall, one minor point. RUNCORN TRUE BLUES V. WIDNES ROVERS.—Tbit match was played at Widnes on Saturday, and after a very pleasant game ended in a win for the Blues, who had only 13 men, by 3 goals, 2 tries. and 8 minor points, to Rovers 1 try and 1 minor point. The tries for the Blues were ob- tained by Booth 2, Hulf 1, Burton. and Howard 3..; Burton kicked the goals. LITHERLAND V. ST. HELENS.—This match was played at Litherland on Saturday. St. Helens were not fully repre- sented, and a miler uninteresting game ended in favour of the home team by a goal and two tries to a try. Teams Sr. Helens:: Gregeon, back.; Telaseldon, Finney, and Pen- ningten, three-quarter backs.; Verley (captain) and Deardon, half backs.; Halton, Rogers, Kershaw, Cirice, Dixon, Pen- ningt in, Borthwick, Edwards, and Heaton, forward, Litheilend : Webster, back; Lycett (ciptain), Johnson, and Holmes, three-quarter backs; Hayworth and Houghton, half backs; Holmes, Harding, McManus, Bold, Richardson, Larkin, Dower, Johnson, and Murphy, forwards. • ST. HELENS V. LITEECRLAND.—Tbesa clubs met for the first time this season at Sr. Helens, on New Year's Day. Upwards of 500 spectators turned up to witness the match. The visitors, who are one of the strongest clubs in the Liverpool district, brought a strong team with them, but St. Helens had only an indifferent team, being minus D. McLaughlin, W. Janice, and C. Ross. The game was evenly contested, and the end resulted in a draw, neither having scored. Lycett, Webster, Holmes, McManus, and Harding for Litherland, and Tickle, Heselden, Pennington, Twist, Borthwick, and Kereltew showing splendid form for their respective sides. Teams—St. Helms.: Tickle, back ; Pennineton, Haseldon, and Gregson, three-quarter backs.; Varley and Deerdora, half-backs; Twist. Borthwick, Fin- ney, itegers, Halton, Bassnett, Grice, Kershaw. and Una- worth, forwards. Litherland : Webster, back; Lycetr, Holmes, and Johnson, three-quarter backs; Larkin and Houghton, half-backs •, Holmes, Harding, McManue, Bold, Richardson, Larkin, Dower, Johnstone. and Murphy, for- wards. RUNCORN V. LIVERPOOL Gruerisnar.—This match was played on Saturday on the ground of the Gymnasium, Sef- ton Park, before a large crowd of spectators. A well-con- tested game resulted in a victory for the visitors by one goal, one try, and three minor points, to one goal and one minor point. Play was commenced shortly after three o'clock, the Gymnasium having the advantage of the wind. Winstanley obtained a try for Runcorn, which was improved upon by Faulkner. After some loose play Edwards collared the Ball, and by a splendid kick registered a goal for the Gymnasium. A try was obtained soon after by Barnes, but the place kick failed. On resuming after half tirne, both sides played up with spirit, but nothing was scored with the exception of a minor point for Runcorn, the game re- sulting as stated above. P. Edwards, E. Coulteurst, and W. t Dutton played well for the home team, while Winstanley, Barnes, Faulkner, and Wainwright may be singled out of j the Runcorn team, although the whole of their forwards I played exceedingly well. There was a fair attendance of spectators, who wit- nessed a good game, the Wanderers winning by four goals to two. GOLBORNE V. STUBSHAW CROSS WANDERERS.—At Go)- borne on Saturday before a large number of spectators. The visitors won the toss and kicked down brow. The visitors scored the first goal in five minutes. On resuming play the vieitors scored another goal. The home team then began to force the play, and up to the end of the game they had the best of it, winuing a pleasant game by five goals to two. Eartensreww V. OSWESTRIC.—These elevens met at Os- westry on Saturday afternoon, when an extraordinary game was played. The Eerlestonians were minus Duxbury and Ogden, the latter of whom has not yet recovered from the injury lee sustained a few weeks ago. The first half of the game was evenly contested, though the home eleven exhi- bited a degree of roughness. When ends were changed the score was one geol to none in favour of the Oewestrians. Daring the remainder of the game the home teartrindalged in rough tactics, the result being that Dagnall, Stine, Elli- son, and other players from Earlestown received severe in- juries. So far as play by the visitors was concerned, it was conspicuous by its absence, and the home players conse- cuently had matters entirely their own way. When time was celled the "score" was—Oswestry, eight goals; Ear- lestown, none. NEwTON COMMON RANGERS (IST) RAYDGCIC (2en),--ThiB match was played on the ground of the latter, on Saturday. The Rangers kicked of against the wind. Clapham was the first t ) score for Haydock, but Wilkinson retaliated. The second half was all in favour of the visitors, the good play of the forwards and passing of the half-backs enabling Derrycott, Waterman, and Dale to score. When time was called the Rangers were victorious by four goals to one. Teams :—Rangers: Thompson, goal; Tyre and J. Worsley, backs; R. Sephton, Dale, and Waterman, half-backs; Wil- kinson and Dorrycott (captain), right wing; Harrison, centre; Morris and Lowe, left wing. Haydock : Hardman, goal; Boardman and W. Worsley, backs; Hilton, Abbott, and Haslehurst, half-backs; J Leivesley and Clapham. right wing; T. Leivesley, centre; Cawley and Davies, left WitliC. H. Worsley officiated as referee. EARLBISTOWN (A Teem) v. NEW SPRINGS (IST TEAII.) This match was played on the ground of tire Earlestown Club on Saturday. The train service being rather awkward the visitors were unable to leave Wigan before 3-10, and consequently the game was'only twenty Lninutes each way. The Earlestown captain being 3nccessfal with the coin Gibson, for Springs, kicked off, and the home forwards im- mediately invading the visitors' quarters won a corner, which. however, proved unsuccessful. The Springs custo- dian kicked out, and tke visitors' right wing pair securing ran cleverly up their wing, but the home team backs landed the sphere a good elistance down the field, anel the Earles- town oentre very soon had the ball between the visi- tors uprights. Restarting from centre the home forwards found the visitors' backs plenty to do, but half time was called with the score standing at one goal to nil in favour of Earlestown. On immediately restarting, the visitors for. wards made an attack on the Earlestown goal, the pressure altinsately ending in Springs equalising the score. Recones mencing, the home team forwards were not long in getting *up to the visitors' goal, and soon registered a second point. The game eventually ended in a victory for Earlestown by two goals to one. Tearns:—New Sprinae : Goal, T. Richards; backs, Price and J. H. Richards; half backs, Lowe, Burton, and Fairhurst; forwards, Ralphs (captain). Lates, Gibson, Hilton, and Taylor. Earlestown: Goal, J. Pope; backs, Unsworth and Saul; half backs, Faircloneh, Harrop, and Fazakerly ; forwards, Holden, James, Turner, Smith, and Roberts. Umpires, Messrs. J. Burton and J. Ogden ; referee, Mr. J. Ellison. EARLUSTOWN V. EARLESTOWN WANDERERS.: EXCITING CCIATEST.—One of the most exciting matches ever played in Zarlestown was witnessed on the ground of the Earlestown Wanderers at Newton Common on New Year's Day, when the Earlestown club and the Wanderers first team met for the first time on that ground. The two teams bad met on the Mesnes, the ground of the first named, on Christmas Day, when the home team won by three goals to none. The return match WAS expected to prove an exciting affair, and the supporters of the :Wanderers had confidently expressed themselves as to the result. There was a large attendance of spectators, notwithstanding the threatening character of the weather. Excitement during the game was very high, and there was a considerable amount of betting. The ground was very unfavourable for apod play, being nearly a foot deep in water and mud in several places. A strong wind blew from goal to goal. Having won the toss, the visitoes' captain elected to play downhill and against the wind. The leather was started by the Wanderers, who had a slight advantage for a few minutes. They ultimately scored amid prolonged cheers, which were again and again renewed when a snored point was registered three minutes later. The Earlestown club representatives still had the worst of the play, and appeared far from being accustomed to the heavy aed uneven ground. Their opponents played with considerable dash, and their supporters loudly cheered i when they notched a third point. The visitors afterwards played in better combination, and the game was of a more even character. The captain slightly altered the positions of some of the players, and this appeared to improve their play. Hard lines met the attempts of the Earlestown club team te score, while Champion kept out one or two danger- ous shots. Shortly before ends were changed the Wanderers forwards bore down on the Earlestown goal, and to the consternation of the supporters of the latter team, with cor- respondingly jubilant shouts and cheers, they scored a fourth goal. Half time was then called, with the score—Wanderers four goals, Earlestown none. A feeling then prevailed that for the first time for a good number of years the Earlestown club would be defeated by another local organisation, and amid increasing excitement the game was renewed. The Liverpool cap holders at once set to work to reduce their opponents' lead, and after some very fast play Earlestown scored their first point, the feat being rewarded with hearty cheers. This success appeared to infuse new energy in the play of the visitors, for nearly the whole of the second half they peened their opponents. The latter were compelled to act on the defensive owing to the severe pressure, but loud cheers announced that another score had been made. Immediately afterwards a desperate scrimmage occurred almost under the cross-bar of the Wanderers' goal, and its defender, Champion, was rolled through along with the ball amid cheers. The referee (Mr. J. B. Porter) disallowed the goal on account of alleged off side play—a questionable,decision which evoked loud hisses and hooting from the spectators. The resumption of the play witnessed another determined rush by the Earlestown forwards, but the attack was repulsed and ea visit paid te the other end. Sims, Ellison, and Dagnall returned the leather, however, and it was finally shot through the goal—the third goal be- ing thus added about fifteen minutes from the close of the game. As only one point divided the scores of the two elevens every subsequent movement of the bell was watched with keen interest, and there were lusty shouts and cheers by the respective partisans. A few minutes before the call of time Champion was called upon to stop seeeral splendid shots, hut despite his utmost exertions Earlestown suc- ceeded in again scoring, and both sides were placed on a level. This was the signal for a prolonged outburst of cheers, while quite contrary to the close of the ,first half of the genie the Wanderers' supporters were very despondent. The remaining few minutes of play were in favour of the Liverpool Cupholders, but no additional point was scored and the match 'thus resulted in a draw of four goals each. The teams were—Earlestown: J. Appleton, goal; R. Green and J. Whalley, backs: J. Duxbury, R. Bowker, and J. Green, half-backs; W. Rich and H. Holcroft, right-wing : A. W. Da.gnall, centre: J. W. Sims and J. Ellison, left- wing. Earlestown Wanderers.: T. Champion, goal; J. Mather and T. Siddeley, backs; W. Ellison, R. Johnson, and L. Lowe, half-backs; J. Kirkham, A. Allen, right-wing; W. Thompson, centre; J. Shaw and W. Shaw, left-wing.

NOTES BY THE WAY. The meeting of Enghind and Wales on Saturday at Blackheath resulted, as was expected, in the defeat of the Welshmen by one goal, two tries, and three minors to one goal and two minors. The Principality- have every reason to be proud of their teamtas they made a gallant struggle for victory; and today, when they meet Scotland, they are Imre to find the Scots a lot of work. The tour of the famous Fettcsians-Loretenians team which commenced on Ftiday when they opposed Manches- ter, a grand game ending in a victory for the colleges by two goals to one goal and one try for the Whalley Range , men. The goal which won the Fettes the match was dropped from field of play after time was up. The point has, therefore, been referred to the Rugby Union for deci- sion. On Saturday they journeyed down to Liscard to tackle Cheshire, whom they, defeated by three goals to one try. Great excitement was evinced in the meeting of Bradford and Wakefield Trinity at Park Avenue. Both teams, though not fully represented, exercised all their abilities to score a victory. After a splendid and evenly-contested game, Bradford were declared the victors by one goal and five minor points to one try and four minors. Quite ten thousand spectators witnessed tbis meeting. The Swinton team of late have been very unlucky, the lion having had his tail pulled on several occasions this season. It was again pulled last Saturday when the Edin- burgh Institution, a very 'powerful team, managed to score a victory by one goal to two tries; rather hard lines for Swinton. Salford went over to Dewsbury; a grand anci•evenly- contested game resulting in the defeat of the Salford men by one try to nil. Broughton received a visit from Rochdale Hornets, but the ineeets had to submit to defeat, the Griffins winning by two goals one try to one try. On New Year's Day Warrington had for their opponents the Bootle club, who came with 'a good reputation, having the previous week defeated Walton, but the home team fairly made rings round them, winning an easy game by two goals and eight tries to nil. Bootle will not forget for some time their visit to Warrington. Warren's men paid the Walkden team a visit on Saturday, but having a weak team could only make a draw of it, the ground and ball being in wretched condition. Runcorn met on New Year's Day Rochdale St. Clements, a capitally-contested gains ending in a draw. 1 On Saturday Widnes met this team also, and contrary to ex ' pectation could only make a draw of it.

An ordinaty meeting of this Council was held in the Council Chamber, Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. There were present the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) presiding; Aldermen Burgess, Levies, Holmes, and Webster; Coun- cillors Greening, Brown, Broadb, nt, Dakin, Dixon, Marsh, Taylor, Aston, Hutchinson, Bolton, Fleming, Tinsley, W. Pierpoint. J. Pierpoint, Litton, Sutton, Whittle, Greenall, and Wright; Messrs. Bro )k (:own clerk), Whittle (deputy town clerk), Longdin (borough surveyor), Paterson (gas manager), and Chorley (borough treasurer).

div.head: NUISANCE.
div.p: A NUISANCE.

The MAYOR moved, and COaaCillOr BROADBENT seconded, the adoption of the \Vetch Committee's minutes. Cduncillor Durieer referred to nuisances in Arpley-street at night, and asked if they could not have a better attend- ance of polioe officers down that street. One gentleman had proposed that those who live in that district should cease to pay rates until they found some attention paid to the nuisance. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Alderman BURGESS called attention to the exposure of furniture for sale in certain parts of the town. Where this , took place. the streets were telerably wide it was true, but it appeared to him an irregular practice, and eventually these people might obtain a right of use to the street. He simply wished to call attention to the fact, and if the Mayor would be kind enough to bring it under the notice of the Watch Committee with the view of its being .inquired into, and, if it were necessary, let the people who were occupying their streets for that purpose pay something. The MAYOR; IS there any particular street? Alderman BURGESS said he would allude to Winwicke street, but that was not the only part of the town. The MAYOR said that, with reference to Councillor Dixon's inquiry, the subject had been brought before the Watch Committee, and the Chief Constable had been com- municated with, but he declared the police were ordered to perambulate that street even more frequently than ordinary. The Chief Constable said he was utterly enable to meet the difficulty that Councillor Dixon spoke of.
The minutes were then e,,nfirmed. FINANCE.

The minutes of the Finance Committee contained a reso- lution that the town clerk give tha necessary notices for the repayment of a large number of mortgages, and that the same be off .red to the mortgagees at the reduced rate of interest of £3 lOs per cent per annum, as from and after the first day of July, 1886, upon applic.tion to the borough treasurer on or before the Ist March, 1886. • Alderman liorasus, in moving the confirmation of the *minutes, said they would probably bent& from the above measure in about six months' time,
Councillor GREENING seconded the adoption of the minutes, which Witti agreed to.
