THE HHALTH OP THE BOROUGH. Alderman BURGESS, in moving the confirmation of the Sanitary Committee's minutes, said there was nothing in the minutes calling for special remark, but he might with the permission of the Council make an announcement which was important, and was very gratifying to the Sanitary Committee. He thought it would gladden the hearts of the ' members of that Council, and every right-thinking person who had an interest in the welfare of Warrington. It was with reference to the death rate of the borough for the past year, which he was happy to tell them was only 18.9 in the 1,000. (Hear, hear.) The first quarter was 21.09, the second 1986,• the third 1667, and the fourth 181. He thought that was a very satisfactory condition of things so far as the health of the town was concerned, and it was very ' pleasing to have an announcement to make that they were progressing at so satisfactory a rate. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR thought that that was a state of things which must be particularly gratifying to Alderman Bur- gess. The minutes were then adopted.

PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE. The minutes of the Paving and Seweraee Comrnittee con- tained the following :—Resolution, that 150 tons of macadam breakers be purchased from Messrs. Clare and Ridgway, at 5s 6cl per ton; resolution, that the sewer out- let at Bank Qaay Wharf be completed to boundary wall river ; recommendation, that the tender of Messrs. Pearson Knowles, Coal and Iron Company, for 200 gullies, accord- ing to sample, and to be delivered free at lie 9d each, be accepted; recommendation, that the tender of Mr. James Savage, of Newry, for the supply of 300 tons of sets, at 15s 6d per ton, delivered in Liverpool, be accepted, subject to the sets being equal to an approved sample to be supplied to the borough surveyor. Alderman aeries moved, and Councillor Memel secon- ded the adoption of the minutes. Councillor BROADBENT called attention to the state of Knutsford-road within the borough. (Hear, hear.) That road was in a very bad condition. He knew there were difficulties in connection with the road; he knew that it was a county road leased to the borough, and that the reason given wby it was not put in thorough repair and made sat- isfactory was that the committee and borough surveyor were afraid that if they spent the sum of money necessary to put the road in good repair the county might resume the care of it, as they did once before, and let it out to the contractor, and allow the road again to sink into an uneat- isfactory condition. He should be very glad if the com- mittee would take the matter into consideration and see whether some aleangemeet that would be mutually satisfac- tory could be made with the county, by which there could be a lease of the road for a number of years to the borough, and then the borough would feel justified in putting the road in thorough repair. Alderman HOLMES asked for a word of explanation as tor the sewer outlet at Bank Quay wharf. Alderman DAVIES said tnat at present there was an outlet at Bank Quay, near the wharf that is occupied by the Cor- poration, and it was deemed necessary to complate that to the boundary well of the river, so as to make it perfect. As regarded the remarks of Councillor Broadbent, when they I entered into an arrangement with the county to take over Knutsforthroad and also Wilderspool-road, they impressed upon them that they should enter into an arrangement with the Corporatnn for a long term, or, if possible, make it permanent, hilt they would give a lease for more than seven years. The county authorities told them at the same time —and he thought the Council might depend upon it—that the Corporation might expect that the road would not be taken out .of their hands at any time. He should ask the Council that the Paving and Sewerage Committee should maintain the road as if it were not going to fall out of their hands, and that they should put it in a proper condition. (Hear, hear.) The road was suffering to some extent from their putting doern the ejection pipes. The surveyor told him that he bad made arrangements for the UB3 of the Highway Board's steam roller. Toe committee admitted the road was not in good condition. The Meeort said that everybody who was in the habit of travelling over that road would receive with pleasure the announcement of Alderman Davies. He thought the road was pretty mealy as bad as anything could be. Councillor WHITTLE : More than half the Council live over the bridge at Latchford. (Laughter.) The minutes were then carried. CEMETERY COMMITTEE. The minutes of this ceminittee, which were approve, contained a report of the reeistrar that the interments for ths past four weeks were :—Adalts 43, minors 51, stillborn and premature 17; and for the corresponding period last year—Adults 62, minors 105, stillborn and premature 11. The receipts for the past six weeks were XBB 5s 11d, and for the corresponding period last year, £B9 7s 4d. museum, LIBRARY, AND ARTS COMMITTEE. The minutes of this, committee were approved on the motion of Councillor W. PIPRPOINT, seconded by Councillor LITTON. They expressed the thanks of the committee to Messrs. George Jeckson, L. Greening, R. Pierpoint, N. Hey- wood, Scott, and Beemont for contributions. In November the visitors to the museum numbered 1,182, the books issued in the reading-room 1,348, and the books issued to subscri- bers 1,650.

RIVERS COMMITTEE. This committee recommended that Alderman Crosfield be appointed chairman, and Councillor Litton deputy-chair- man, for the ensuing year; and that Alderman Davies be re-appointed to represent the Council on the Uppor Mersey Navigation Commission. The report was adopted on the proposition of Alderman DAVIES, seconded by Councillor DARIN. TOWN HALL, PARR, AND BATHS COMMITTEE. 1 The MAYOR proposed, and Councillor JOHN PIERPOINT seconded, the adoption of the minutes of this committee. which recommended that the main walk in the recreation ground, from Crobfiild-street to Kendrick-street, be re-laid in a permanent manner with limestone chipping, and as- phalte, and reported that the income from the baths for the past four weeks was £3 10s, as against £2 17s the correspon- ding weeks last year. Alderman HOLMES suggested that the vinery in the gar- dens should be made into a conservatory, which might prove attractive to the public. The expense of maintaining the present vinery was more than the value of the fruit. Councillor Jon)? PIERPOINT said that would entail con.

siderable expense, as the present glass would not be suitable fer the purpose. He thought, however, that it might easily be converted into a propogating house. . Councillor BOLTON expressed himself in accord with the views of Alderman Holmes. He thought that if the vinery was converted into a conservatory, or something else at which the people might look inside, it would be bene- ficial.

CJuncillor SurroN said that it would perhapa be the best plan to convert the vinery into a greenhouse, and he sug- gested that steps be taken to ascertain the probable cost. Councillor VV. PIERPOINT said that, as there was an in- crease in the receipts at the Baths, he hoped that the com- mittee would not lose sight of the unsAtisfactory state of the Baths, and that they would do what they could to furnish the people of Warrington with a bath that would be a credit to the town.
Councillor GREENING thought it would be well if the committee considered whether it would be desirable to change the present vinery into a greenhouse or a propagat- ing house _ .

-Councillor WHITTLE said that this business was some- thing like the erection of the "bird cage" in the Market for the office of the Inspector, which when furnished would net cost much less than £3OO. They had got the place roofed in and a skylight over it, so thdt in summer the In- spector would be roasted alive. (Laughter.) He ought t% have been roasted alive before, and so ought every Corpora- tion official in the town. (More laughter.) After a few remarks from the Mayor, the minutes were approved.
XLMEETS COMMITTEE: TEE INSPECTOR'S OFFICE.

The confirmation of the minutes of this committee. which recommended the acceptance of a tender of Mr. J. S. Gar- land for spiral staircase at the inspector's office at £lO 10s, was proposed by Councillor LITTON and seconded by Coun- cillor Jonte PIERPOINT. Councillor BOLTON asked whetker there were any more " extras " to be required for the inspector's office. Councillor Wurrrix asked why did they want to spend £3OO en an office of that description; an old railway waggon would have served a private firm for such a pur- pose. The Corporation would not spend their own money in that way. The Markets Committee bad always been con- sidered the "committee of mistakes." They were the biggest duffing committee he ever came acress; they were a lot 'of old women. (Laughter.) The MaYon I must say that is a very grave reflection upon the women. (Laughter.) Councillor Lrrrox said he thought they might treat Councillor Virhittle's remarks with the contempt they de- served. For the iron staircas., he believed, the original esti- mate was something like £25, and it was now being reduced to £lO. Therefore the estimates were decreased, and the 'dulling committee" knew their busiaess better than the duffers.who addressed th,m. Tke minutes were confirmed. OAS COMMITTER.
The confirmation of the minutes of this committee was moved by Alderman HOLMES and seconded by Alderman WESTER. _ _

Alderman HOLMES. in answer to observations made by Councillor Dixon with regard to deposits being required by the Gas Committee, said that he should have had notice given him that the question would be brought up. It was one of considerable delicacy, and unless there was something grievously wrong cases should not be brought before the Ciouncil in that way. .

The MAYOR remarked that the Gas Company allowed in- terest on deposits. It was a delicate questios to say of whom deposits should or should not be required. As far as he had seen the greatest consideration had been shown to those who had been called upon to make deposits. The minutes were confirmed. _ GENERAL PORPOSES CJIMITTLE.

The minutes of this committee, which were approved on the motion of the MAYoR, seconded by Councillor BROAD• BENT. reported the appointment of a sub-committee to act as a Parliamentary Committee, and to be composed of the Mayor, Aldermen Burgess, Holmes, Davies, Pickmere, and Webster, and Councillor Milner. They also contained a • resolution to the Effect that the Mayor, Alderman Holmes, Davies., and Kean. and Councillors Broadbent and Platt be appointed a sub-committee to report as to the most appro- priate phces to be secared by the Corporation for the pur- pose of forming open spaces and recreation grounds in the borough.

THE ECCENTRICITIES OF GAS METERS. Councillor WILLIAM PIERPOINT proposed, "That as dis- putes do arise with reference to over-charges in the gas consumers' accounts, it be an instruction to the Gas Com- mittee to devise some means for the settlement of such dis- .

putes in a fair and equitable manner." He remarked that in proposing the motion he had no antagonistic feelings to the Gas Committee, the officials, or at4y on. He had made the motion as wide as he could so that there might be a fair, a free, and a full discussion. After asking the members of the committee for the moment to divest themselves of that particular character, and consider the matter simply as members of the Council representing. the .ratepayers, Mr.

Pierpoint said that they would agree With him that, as was I the case between private firms and their customers, disputes did arise. ne quoted a case that occurred in 1884, when a contract with a private trader was cancelled by the Gas Company, because in the sale of the article he had con- tracted to purchase the market went against him. That action was a very fair one, but he thought that if the com- mittee could settle disputes with one class of their cus- tomers they could apply the same principles with regard to another class. Haying cited another instance of a dispute) settled, the mover of the resolution said that if they ad- mitted the principle that disputes would arise, and that it was better not to drive too hard a bargain in settling those disputes, he would like to call their attention to one or two cases of as accounts. He had one example which he

thoaght that he could vouch for. It was an account paid bv a widow lady, most regular in her habits. He would fairly take one year as another, especially when there had been no extraordinary circumstances that would cause an increase in the consumption of gas. In the winter half-year of 1883 there was a gas consumption of 9,700 feet. In the corresponding period of 1884, when the family burned the sane amount of gas, the meter registered 4,500 feet, and in the winter half-year of 1885 there were 15,000 feet regis- tered. He bad another account of a gas meter's registra- tions for the last four years. In the summer halts of the years the following number of feet were registered :—ln 1882 3,600. in 1883 3,700, in 1884 4.800, and in 1885 19,800. For the first three years there was thus an average consumption of 4,033 feet, with an aver- age charge, including meter rent, of 163 41, whilst the money charge for the last year was 103 10d. This was rather a serious charge for a man in a small way of business, who had based his calculations as to what the charge would be on previous charges. In such cases a person complained to the gas officials, the meter was examined, and he was afterwards told that it was quite right, the gas had been used, and he would have to pay for it. What did they do in the case where a gentleman in the town was rendered an account for over £3O and said he would not pay it. The same process was gone through, but the gentleman did not Day. He engaged a solicitor, with the result that the pay- ment was ultimately based upon the average of the two or three years preceding. The account was nearly £35, the amount paid was about £lO, and the consumer paid £5 in legal expenses. If there was arbitration for the rich consumer there should also be arbitration for the peer one. He suggested that the inspection of meters should be as close as possible, and that a card should be supplied to consumers on which the state of the index of the meter at the time of the inspector's visit could immedi- ately be entered. The consumer would at ones see if there was any great increase of consumption going on. It would act as a cheque on wasteful censumptiott or defective fit tinge. Councillor JOHN PIERPOINT seconded the resolution. Coancillor DIXON said that he remembered one case in which gas had escaped through defective fittings and the committee took the responsibility. He had no doubt that defective fittings caused much waste. Councillor FLEMING supported the resolution. Councillor Surroer thought that toe best way was for everyone to examine their own meters. Alderman HOLMES said that he bad no objection to the question being ventilated. No meter was ever sent out from the gas works without having the seal of the govern- ment inspector upon it, which proved that it was a correct recording instrument. He believed also that it was true that no aas was registered that had not been consumed, and if there was any error it was a fact that it was in faveur of the cousutners themselves. The meter was the only um- pire to which they could appeal, and if these extraordinary discrepancies were frequent there might be some reason why they should accept the resolution, bat he had ascer- tained that only one or two such cases occurred during the year. If that was the case was it necessary to pass such a stringent resolution. He would at once accept the proposal to have tickets and might say that even now tickets were used by many of the manufacturers of the town. When the gas had passed through the meter they had a right to charge for it. They were reasonable men and did not de- sire to be tyrannical- with their customers. Alderman BURGESS suggested that it be imperative on inspectors to leave a record of what was regis- tered after making an inspec'ion. Ho might men- tion that in his honee, in the summer of 1880, the gas consumption was 10,000 feet ; in 1881 it was 13,600 ; in 1882 it was 16,800; and in 1883 it was 20,200. (Laugh- ter.) After submitting these figures to the Gas Committee in 1883 the consumption fell in 1884 from 20,200 feet to 16.700 feet, without anything being done to the meter, or with regard to leakages. But the strangest thing was that in 1884 he had the gas fittings taken out of two rooms, aboat one third of the whole, and in 1885, notwithstanding this, there was an increase from 16,700 to 18,702—(laugh- ter)—although there was no leakage. There was something in the action of gas meters that was not easy to understand He would go no further in removing burners from his house—(more laughter)—for if he removed all the meters he would, according to 'what had occurred, have about twice as much to pay. He was content to let it alone. He knew that the engagements of the Gas Committee had to be met by someone, and it required a little patriotism on the part of someone to acquiesce in matters of that kind. He thought that there was satisfactory cause for some in- quiry. He entirely exonerated the committee and the officiate of any irregularity, but thought something wanted inquiring into and remedying if possible, Councillor BROADBENT thought the Council must be obliged to Councillor W. Pierpoint for bringing the matter forward. It was not only desirous that justice should be done to consumers, but tliat they should be satisfied that justice wias done to them. It was one of those cases where the seller had it all his own way, as he held the scales in the shape of a meter and charged for the scales as well.

, Although it might be said they could keep a record and examine the meter, very few people did so. He had no doubt that in tbis case the seller was much more 'conscien- tious that were many manufacturers, but he should be glad if, where there were such obvious increases as to make it almost impoesible that the gas could have, been consumed, the consumer who suffered should be able to have some appeal. He could see that there were difficclties in the way, and hoped that on tbat occasion Mr. Pierpoint would taot press his motion in the exact terms in which it stood, for he could quite b,lieve that such an one would be embarras- log to the Gas Committee. Mr. Pierpoint had got an adr vantage by his motion in the discussion that had folowed, and in the promise from the chairman of the c mtmittee that cards should be adopted, and that the inspector should be instructed to record on each the consumption of gas that had taken place on the premiees.
Councillor W. PIERPOINT said that with the censent of his sec•nder he would withdraw his motion.—The seconder consented, and the motion was then withdrawn. This concluded the business.

div.head: WARRINGToN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGToN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of tills Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present— The Rev. G. F. Roberts (chair...lan), Messrs. Harrison, Broadbent, Blackhurst, Darbyshire, Brown, Gibson, W. Houghton, Ratcliffe, Humphries, J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. Sutton (deputy clerk). THE PADGATE sciropm. At a meeting of the Schools tommittee, an estimate of Messrs. Collin and Son was submitred for 80 window blinds completed and painted for the sum of 3s. each to sample, and it was resolved to accept it providing the timber be of yellow pine and the painting be of three coats. The com- mittee passed a vote cordially thanking Messrs. Darbysbire, Crompton, and Lawless, and also to Mrs. A.ppleton, of Bruche Hall, for gifts to the children. The Superintendent was authorised to order from the Warrington Corporation the necessary gas fittings and lamps for the children's yard and play sheds, viz., one Bray's lamp for centre of yard, four shed or bracket lamps, one stable lamp, and two lamps to be placed at the approach to the school ' rooms.—Mr. BLACKIIIIIIST and Mr. GREENING expressed a hope that these lamps would be used carefully, so that waste might be prevented.—The minutes were adopted.

div.head: TER CHRISTMAS DINNER.
div.p: TER CHRISTMAS DINNER.

Mr. MACKAY, the mastei of the Workhouse, reported that the Christmas festivities had passed off most satisfactorily. Nearly 400 inmates partook of the dinner in the large dining hall, the remainder who were unable to come having it in their respective rooms. The beer used was 145 quarts, in- cluding the little that was given to those Oro sat up the previous night prepAring the pudding, ccoking, &c. The fruit was used (except MI bs) for mince meat, puddings. .ic„ for the inmates and ufficrs, and this small quantity will be used with discretion and judgment in the puddings for the sick. A lady who took great interest in the House, visiting the sick in all weathers, kindly sent each patient a Christmas card. Mr. Jolley and Mr. Little sent a lot of illustrated and comic papers ; Mr. Lawless and Mr. Robert Heaton a box of oranges each, for which he (Mr. Mackay) thanked them very much. He wished also to record his thanks to the officers for their hearty co-operation and assis- tance in the work, and it would be satisfactory to the Guar- dians to know that everything p>.ssed off without a hitch of any kind, and all seemed to enjoy themselves thoroughly without excess, the good order and conduct being remark- able throughout. There are 419 inmates to-day (January &h).—The CHAIRMAN said he was very glad to see that the dinner passed off satisfactorily. He should have been glad to be present himself, but unfortunately he was de- tained elsewhere, having his duties as a clere,vman.—Mr. GREENING said that the return as to the number who par- took of the Christmas dinner at the workhouse, Sic., had not been given as directed by the Board.—Mr. BROWN said that was the only report he had seen; if it did not answer what they wanted they should send it back again and ask the• Master to give further details.—Mr. GREENING said the report in the book did not answer to the resolution of the Board.—The CHAIRMAN said that perhaps Mr. Brown would see that it was Aupplemented with further particulars.—Mr. Bucewer assented to this.—Mr. BLACKIIIIRST asked why the return was not according to the resolution.—Mr. BROAD- BENT remarked that the return stated all the fruit had been used within a few pounds.—Mr. GIBSON : I should like to know how much has been used for mince meat and how much for plum pudding. (Liuglater.)—Mr. ReerctaFFE I think you are mixing the thing now. (Laughter.)—Mr. GREENING said he only wanted to know the ournber-of people who partook of the dinner, and the quantity con- sumed.—Mr. RATCLIFFE said he had been present at the dinner, and he believed everything had been served out judiciously.—Mr. GREENING remarked that he was not objecting to aeything, or imputing metives to anyone; all he wanted was the return the Board had ordered to be made.—Mr. DARBYSIIIHE said he should like the return to be made in an intelligible form to satisfy the minds of those who asked for it. He saw that in other Unions returns bad been given of how much fruit had been used, ia what way it had been used, and he did not see why that Union could not be supplied with the information it required in a ' form that could be understood at once.—The CHAIRMAN said Mr. Brown had signified his willingness to supply them with the information they wanted, and he would no doubt draw it up in such a form as to satisfy them all.—Mr. BROWN said the Committee would endeavour to give such information as would satisfy any reasonable person, but beyond that they could not undertake to go.—The CHAIR- MAN : That is all that is asked for. - - -
The report of Mr. Mines, the superintendent of Padgate Schools, was also read, and stated that the Christmas dinner at that establishment had passed off in a most satisfactory manner.
SCHOOL FEES.

The School Fees Committee reported that there had been 41 applications for fees allowed, 30 of which were old and 11 new cases.—On the motion of Mr. BROWN, seconded by Mr. GREENING, the minutes were adopted.

div.head: PENWORTHAII BRIDGE.
div.p: PENWORTHAII BRIDGE.

The CLERK reported that as the result of the memorial to the Lancashire Annual Sessions of the Guardians against the erection of Penwortham Bridge at the expense of the county further progress with the proceedings in connection with the bridge had been stopped by the decision of the Ses- sions. Particulars of the discussion at the Sessions were given in our issue last week.—The Citexaman said the con- elusion was very satisfactory. (Hear, hear.)—The CLERK suggested that a vote of thanks to the Annual General Sessions for their consideration of the Board's memorial should be passed, and that they should also 1e asked that, in the event of any further proceedings being contempla- ted, they would communicate with that Beard prior to the Annual Session.—The CHAIRMAN moved that that be done. Mr. HARRISON seconded. Mr. BROAD- MENT, in supporting the resolution, said they were indebted to the intelligence and great interest which their Clerk took in matters pertaining to that Board and to the county. He thought it was not too much to say thet if it had not been for the vigilance of Mr. Sutton that scheme would have been carried through and the county would have had to pay for what did not properly belong to it. (Hear, hear.) Therefore it would be a great pleasure to him and he was sure to them all to express their thadis to the Cierk for the services he had rendered, not only to that Beard, but to the whole county.—The CHAIRMAN quite agreed with Mr. Broadbent, but as a matter of fact they. hid already passed a vote of thanks to the Clerk for his action in that metter. —Mr. DARBySHIRE supported the remarks if Mr. Broad- bent.—Mr. BROWN did not see why they should contribute to the £5,000 already expended im connection with the bridge —The CLEnec, in replying, said it was a matter of satisfaction that right should prevail in that mat- ter. It was clearly wrong to build a bridge and provide extensive approaches in a municipal borough (Preston) that was exempt entirely from contributing to bridges in this neighbourhood or any other bridges in the county, whereas in the borough of Warrington they were now widening the ancient approaches to their bridge at an expense to the borough which would likely not be less than £20,000. It was wrong that•Warrington should have to widen its own approaches and pay for its own improvements, Preston not contributing a penny; and yet that Preston was to be exempt for the cost of its own approaches, and actually to he paid for land which it now possessed. (Rear, hear.)— The CHAIRMAN said that one of the magistrates at the annual sessions said that the whole thing had been got up by Mr. Bleckly, hut this statement he entirely contradicted. It was the Guardians who approached Mr. Bleckly. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. GREENING was glad the chairman hat men- tioned that matter. Mr. Bleckly certainly did not make any overtures to that Board to go into the matter. They ought, however, to feel obliged to Mr. Sleekly for his con- duct. (Hear, hear.)—The motion proposed by the chair- man was then carried. This concluded the business of public interest.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JANUARY St, 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JANUARY St, 1886.

PARLIAMENT is IO be called upon to do something.besides consider the queseion of Home Rule for Ireland. The advocates of female suffrage for Parliamentary as for Municipal Elections are determined to be heard. They have requested Mr. WooDALL to take the earliest opportunity of introduc- ing his bill on the subject; and.they are con- fident that the new House of Commons will show itself more favourable to their claims than that which has just passed out of ex- istence. They count, in fact, upon finding a majority in their favour, and they have been pretty careful in making out iheir estimate. It is asserted that, out of the 670 members of the present House of Commons, as many as 314. may be described as friends of the movement. Of known opponents, there are 1 04. ; and, if half only of the zsz whose views are as yet an unknown quantity give their support to the bill, it will be seen that it will secure a safe conduct through the House of Commons. There can be no question as to the progress made by the Society for Women's Suffrage. From being laughed at or pooh-poohed, the advocates of a female franchise have become an important factor in politics. They have carried their point in securing the privilege to vote for members of Town Councils, and it is now simply a ques- tion of time as to the same class being placed on the Parliamentary register. Mr. GLAD' STONE felt that the women's suffrage advoca- tes were somewhat in the way when he was struggling to get the Franchise Bill through the last Parliament. However much he maY have been inclined to take them aboard, he knew that their presence would greatly increase the chances of shipwreck, and, like a wise Captain, he refused to endanger his vessel by overloading. The result justified his judgment; but there are Rachels who re- fused to be comforted because, as they urge, they have been worse treated than HODGE, tbe labourer. It certainly is a grievous anomaly that the widow, say, of a large farmer—a woman employing, directing and paying a number of laliourers, should be everything to the agricultural eye, but noth- ing in the eye of the law when the time comes for appointing law-makers. But we have a great many grievous anomalies; and we are slow to get rid of them. Let the women take'courage ; if °the old Parliament was indifferent, there is more hope of the new. If Mr. Gr...A.DsToNE prudently puts them back one year, he meantime paves the way for their going forward the next year. Let those who would condemn the course he took reflect that if the Franchise Bill had I failed, as it might have failed, by the impor- tation of the female element, the passion and prejudice of the male sex would have ,been excited to such an extent that the advocates of women's suffrage would have been driven to the wall for some time to come. This would, of course, have been very unreason- able; but women are not alone in doing un- reasonable things when excitement takes possession of humanity. It is a noteworthy circumstance in connec- tion with the women's suffrage movement that it is not a party question in the usual acceptation of the term. It is true that the pioneers were Liberals, and that the present leaders are for the most part Liberals; but it is not to be denied that there are many Conservatives who are Reformers in this par- ticular matter. The reason for this is not far to seek; it is pretty generally conceded that the Tories have gained strength by the addi- tion of women to the Municipal Registers. and it is not unnaturally hiferred that the same majority will vote for Conservative candi- dates for seats in the House of Commons. This is a comforting doctrine to the Tories, and we do not doubt that it has silenced many' who:jiave in the past been bitter in their opposition. On the other hand, it accounts. for the indifference that certain Liberals. show to the movement. They do not denY that having gone the length of putting women on one register, it is illogical to op- pose their being placed on another; but they think that women having waited so long rnaY wait a little longer without taking any karni- This may not be very generous; but pollticians are not generous as a rule in dealing with those who are regarded as possible op- ponents. As :BYRON confessed, "Man to. man so oft unjust is always so to woman. That has been the rule of the past; but tile new departure in the advocacy of woman's rights—open as it has been to the laugh of. the scorner—has already effected a great change for the better; and for ourselves we

cannot but think, dismissing for the moment considerations of party politics, that the ex- tension of the suffrage to women will, in the future, better the condition alike of men and women. Those who look ahead per- ceive that the time of Parliament is likely to be employed more than it has been with Social questions—questions which imme- diately concern the everyday life of women, and in which they ought certainly to have a voice. Why are the terms of divorce, for instance, harder for the wife than for the hus- band? Why should the man who commits adultery be able to set his wife .at defiance, if she cannot also prove cruelty, while the husband can obtain a divorce if he can Prove adultery alone? It is because laws made by one class on behalf of another are tever wholly just,

If self the wavering balance shake, It's rarely right adjusted. IV.hat a reflection it is upon our boasted civil- isation and ehristianity that it is only within the past few years that married women have b. een put in a position to protect themselves in matters of property against the ravages of drunken and worthless husbands! It is the Women to-day who are the greatest sufferers from the curse of the drink traffic; and who •Can doubt that it their influence were brought tO bear in national politics it would, in the long run, be on the side of tempennce, and peace, and social purity. But it ought to be sufficient that the claim is a just one to make Parliament willing to concede it. Mrs. SCATCHERD, of Leeds, speaking on the question a few weeks since, said :—" Many Y.„°ung men whom she had taught in the ?unday school, and tried to help .on in life, liar' votes, for it was practically open to any Young man, who might be living with his Parents, to get on the register. These young inen lightly gave their votes and helped to make the laws which their mothers and teachers had to obey." This, she said, was an absurdity, and there is no denying the truth of her statement. We must get rid of the anomaly—as soon as we can. We have given expediency sufficient play; it is ex- Pedient now to be just.

MR. HERBERT GLADSTONE has at last found it necessary to protest against the statements that have been made that he speaks on be- half of his father in the opinions he has expressed on the Home Rule question. The Conservatives have shown themselves not a little irritated at finding that all they can lay hold of by way of warrant for the fuss they have been mailing over Mr. GLADSTONE'S s,tlPPosed opinions on Home Rule is some- ntning which has been said by Mr. HERBERT kiLADSTONE. Mr. FINCH-HATTON, M.P.,

varied the proceedings the other day by in- sinuating that the son was not expressing his ~c'Nvn views; he was being put forward by the lather in order to test the feeling of the country. Replying to a correspondent who had called his attention to this, Mr. HER- BERT GLADSTONE says : " Mr. Finch-Hatton is clearly wrong in his sur- raise, seeing that my views on the Irish question Were quoted and commented on in the last Parlia- laent with some frequency. The Conservatives be- -I.(,)re the election refrained from attaching any B.,!..gnificance to them, for they were at work to con- .„9tiate the Irish party in order to get their votes. 'OW that they have profited by Irish support, they are endeavouring to pose as the patriotic party by raising an anti-Irish cry, and so they pretend that ,111), views on the Irish question are quite new, and gave been put forward to test public opinion, not on 113 r own behalf. This manoeuvre is transparently lishonest. i'his is a crushing rejoinder, and it comes in the nick of time. It will not stop the rank and file of the Tory party from repeating what Mr. FINCH-HATTON has said; but it Will, it is to be hoped, close the mouths of niernbers of Parliament who were disposed to Inake unworthy use of an unworthy cry. It is a curious turn of things that after trafficking for and obtaining the Irish vote, the Tories should be wroth with the son of the leader of the Liberal party because he still adheres to the advanced views he has previously expres- sed on the Irish question. It illustrates bet- ter than anything else could the mistake which Irishmen made who voted Tory. Their leaders are now in danger of making another Inistake—that of demanding too much. It is Well,of course, to have a margin to bargain upon; but on the other hand terms may be sugges- ted so unreasonably high as to shut out the Possibility of a bargain. At a meeting in , Dublin, on Monday, of the Irish National , League, Mr. HARRIS, M.P., is reported to have said that "they should have such per- fect freedom to take the whole country into - their management, as would enable Ireland to assume a position among the nations, ar- ranging her commercial relations with Eng- land and the rest of the world, developing Manufactures by protective measures, and imposing taxes upon persons who elec- ted to use English instead of Irish goods." I)emands of this kind should, we think, be met, as soon as possible, with the statement Of a united Parliament that they cannot be entertained. If the Tories believe in Pro- tection, that is another matter; let them say and begin, if they dare, by trying to tax zoods which are sent to Ireland. kilit we -do not believe they are " so far gone ;" Fair Trade is to be humoured as "a Pious opinion" in order to catch votes; but there are no signs, as yet, of the Government 13eing disposed to back up the imposture by egislation. The Liberals have a just con- tempt for the craze' and will not allow Ireland any form of Home Rule which, commencing With a war of tariffs, would end in a civil bar. Whatever is done in the direction of ihome Rule, or local self-government, Eng- land must take care of herself, and she must, too, take care of Ireland.

THE Arabs, who had agairibecome trouble- some, have been beaten back in the Soudan, and the Jingoes are beginning to talk of going f°rward to Khartoum. Reinforcements are being sent to Egypt, and if the present , '-'nvernment were assured' of a lease of power lt is extremely likely that they would plunge into a terrible war with the Soudanese. ut they are in a minority to begin with; they 'lave difficulties nearer home, and they know lint what to do. Still, the people of this (311ritry require to be vigilant. Two or three successful fights would whet the appetite for /4,ar ; and there is nothing so pleasing to a ory Government as to be able to find an ex- -Ise for doing nothing at home by directing 't`tention to the slaughter of innocents abroad. It should be remembered, too, that the present Government are being specially , `e!npted. They represent the party that ...talsed the cry of "on to Khartoum," and again and again pronounced against Mr. LADsToNE's administration for not taking earlier action with bayonets and big guns. A titulicy of some sort must, of course, be adop- ; and when a General is in the field, and oushed with victory, it is usually a forward Ile- Now is the time for the Government to decide, if they have not already decided, what they will do, and how far they will go

fin following the Arabs along the banks of the Nile. If we are to take Wady Haifa as the boundary line, let us by all means hold it; and the sooner the natives know that we shall hold it at all cost, the better it will be for them and us. But Egypt should pay the piper. It is too much to ask the British Par- liament to find m-n and money in the defence of people who seem to be incapable of de- fending themselves We must mind what we Are about; the sands of the Soudan will swallow up all the blood and treasure we can send, and there may be nothing to show for either, in the end. There is glory to be sure; but it is a poor sort of glory which comes of killing brave men who are fighting for their country and their kind.

div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

, WIDNES YOUNG MEN'S BIBLE CLASS.—The quarterly tea took place on Tuesday night, about fifty persons being present. An enjoyable entertainment followed. ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—George Moles;' son of the signal- man at the Central station this week fell down in Victoria- road, and broke his leg in two places. Mr. Saul attended to the injuries of the boy. SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES —Elizabeth Egan, who resided in Nelson-street, died on Tuesday morning during a severe attack of coughing. The woman had suffered from bronchitis for about two years. The Coroner deemed it un- necessary to hold an inquest. RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB —ln the Cheshire team which meets Northumberland at Newcastle-on-Tyne to-day there are included six members of Runcorn Football Club, viz., Messrs. H. C. Speakman, three-quarter back; H. Hughes, half-back; J. Lewis, W. H. Broady, W. Hughes. and F. G. Joule, forwards. SAMARITAN LODGE 1.0.G.T., WIDNES.—Abont fifty members of this Good Templars organisation sat down to an excellent supper at the Lodge Room, Victoria-road, on Monday evening. Subsequently a very pleasant time was spent in a sociable fashion. The "sisters" had manage- ment of the affair. • WESLEYAN TEMPERANCE SOCIETY, WIDNES.—A meeting under the auspices of the Oakland-street Gospel Temper- ance Mission took place in the school-room on Tuesday evening. There was a good attendance. Mr. J. Duxhury, of Halebank, presided, and delivered an address. Mr. D. Houghton, of Warrington, also spoke, §nd a programme of songs and recitations followed. AGED PEOPLE'S TREAT AT RUNCORN.—From our an- nouncement columns it will be seen that the annual treat to aged persons will take place on the 20th inst. In conse- quence of various representations it has been decided to give tickets on this occasion only to those in poor circum- stances, but other aged people desirous of being present at the interesting gathering will be admitted on payment of one shilling. ROBBERY AT HALE.—At Widnes Police Court, on Mon- day, Thomas Barber, a laboerer, was charged with stealing a goose worth 6e, the property of John Hughes, carter, Pepper-lare, Elate. The goose was missed from the ship- pon early on Friday morning, the Ist mat, and Hughes went to Liverpool where he discovered that the prisoner, who had been in his employ, had sold the bird for 4s to Wm. James Powell, the barman of a public-house in Ad- miral-street. When apprehended by P.C. Clarke the pri- soner admitted his guilt, and said he would not have done it but fer the drink. A CONFIRMED YOUNG THIEF AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Michael Kelly, 16 years of age, was charged with stealing on the 22nd ult. two pairs of trousers, the property of Michael Boyle, of Grenfell- street. The prisoner, when apprehended by P.C. McMas- tera, was wearing a pair of the trousers, and alleged that he had received them from Patrick Burns, 15 years of age. Burns put into the box denied this.—lnspector Wood said the prisoner was a very bad character, and read a long list of offences committed by the prisoner, the last being a larceny, for which he served a month's hard labour.—He was now sentenced to two month's hard labour

FIRE AT WESTON POlNT.—About eight o'clock on Thursday night a fire occurred at the works of the Mersey Salt and Brine Company, Weston Point. The contractor, Mr Becketf, of Hartford, had erected wooden buildings used as offsee, joiners' shop, and smithy, and the fire originated in the office through, it is supposed, the overheating of a small stove. Two young men named Hayes and Mac Lean first observed the flames, and an alarm soon brought the workmen to the spot, and the fire was quickly extin4uished by water from the canal. The office was almost totally destroyed with the contents—plans and important docu- ments. The Runcorn fire brigade went with despatch to the spot, but their services were not required. Superintendent Leah, Inspector Millington, Sergeant Egerton, and a force of constables were present, and rendered every possible as- sistance. The damage is estimated at £6O. FIRE AT WIDNES.—On Wednesday evening about half. past six a fire Woke out in the front room of the house of Mr. C. Powell, hairdresser and musician, Church-street. Mr. Powell, who . has been in delicate health, went un- stairs to give his daughter a lesson on the piano, and ob- serving the room full of smoke called his wife. Mrs. Powell threw open the windows, and perceiving the bed was on fire, pulled off the clothes and mattress, and sent them through the window. In doing so she severely burned her hands and arms, and afterwards fainted. Neighbours ap- peared on the scene and quickly extinguished the flames with buckets of water. It is thought that some soot had accumulated at the back of the chimney, became ignited, and set fire to one of the beams underneath the fire place; as on pulling up the boards of the floor it was found that one of the rafters was nearly burnt through. The damage to the furniture, &c., is stated to be about ;£4O. The goods as well as the building is insured in the Alliance Office. flu/WORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS—Mt. Mclntyre pre- sided over the fortnightly meeting held on Tuesday. Pre- sent—The Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J. Lockwood, and J. J. Bryant ; Messrs. P. Speakman, E. Aaron, W. Whittaker, Highfield, Hewitt, Baguley, Warburton, J. G. Hamilton, Hadfield, Percival, and the Clerk (H. Liriaker). The only matter of interest was the poor rate return for the year sub- mitted by the Clerk. It showed that the expenditure of the Union was £20.131. Of this amount £19,413 was charged upon the common fund of the Union. For in maintenance there had been expended £1,435; outdoor re- lief, £3,599; other expenses connected with relief. £788; maintenance of lunatics, £752; medical relief, £397 ; school attendance expenses, £lll. The contribution to police rate was £4,668, and the outstanding balance of loans was stated to be £2,708.—0n the motion of the Rev. J. Lockwood, seconded by Mr. Speakman, accounts amounting to £BB3 9s 7d were passed for payment, as recommended by the Finance Committee.

C.E.T.S. DEMONSTRATION AT FARNWORTH.-011 Satin day the Now Year's demonstration of the Farnworth Branch of the Church of England I.emperance Society was held. The members assembled at the National .Schools, and, form- ing in procession, walked through the principal thorough- fares of the town, accompanied by the Rev. G. Bond and Mr. J. W. Davies. The Widnes C.E.T.S. brass band and the Farnworth temperance drum and fife band, the latter appearing for the first time, took part In the proceedings. The procession called at the residences of Mrs. Hibbert, Mr. J. Brock, J.P., Mrs. Deacon (Appleton House), Captain Brunner, Mr. E. Carey, and others. In the Parish Church a special service was held, which was well attended. The sermon was preached by Dr. Harrison, of St. Silas's, Liver- pool. A public tea meeting was held in the evening, at the National School, which had been neatly decorated for the occasion. The programme, which consisted of glees, read- ings, songs, and recitations, was gone through in an excel- lent manner by the following ladies and gentlemen :-- Misses Bond, Fogg, Hibbert ; Messrs. B. Thompson, A. G. Davies, F. Lea, D. Lea, W. Browne, J. T. Knowles, F. C. Davies, G. W. Davies, and others. An instructive and eloquent address on the principles of the Church of Eng- land Temperance Society was given by Mr. J. T. Campbell, of Liverpool. At the termination of the proceedings votes of thanks were given. FLAT ROBBERIES AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court on Wednesday, John Carroll, a young man, was charged with breaking and entering into a flat in Widnes Dock. Inspector Ward remarked that there had been several robberies of a similar character recently. On this occasion three woollen guernseys, a pair of trousers, and other arti- cles had been stoles. William Webb deposed that he was captain of the fiat Washington, which was lying in Widnes Dock. On Saturday afternoon everything was secured, but on Monday morning when he returned the cabin had been completely overhauled, and the articles stolen were worth about 30s. P.C. Holbrook stated that he apprehended the prisoner on the previous day in Water-street. He was wearing the stolen trousers. The prisoner was remanded until Monday so that inquiries could be made.—At Widnes Court on Thersday, Joh'? Hayes was charged on suspicion with breaking and entering the fiat Washington, and steal- ing a pair of trousers and three guernseys. He was wearing a pair of stolen braces when apprehended by P.C. Holbrook, and in the house he occupied a knife also stolen from the flat was found. A large quantity of the stolen property was also discovered. He was remanded until Monday.—law- rence Keating, a youth, was charged with breaking into the flat Clarence, lying in West Bank Dock. On the 28th ult. a pair of boots and a flannel singlet were stolen from the fiat, and subsequently the boots were foun iil n the possession of the prisoner. He was remanded.
