RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.—On Monday there was only one case down for hearing---,1 charge of assault against a husband—and it was adjourned. 'I his speaks well for the good conduct of the inhabitants during the fe,tive season. A DRUNKEN BEGGAR AT WIDNES —On Wednesday, at Widnes Court, Margaret Kenntdy. a respectably-dressed elderly woman, was charged with begging on the previous afternoon. Inspector Wood said the wo.nan was at present under police supervision. For several years she had been in the habit of coming to the town on begging excursions, and then got drunk with the money she had received. She had been four times convicted before the local magistrates, and she was now committed to gaol for 14 days with hard labour. I CRUEL FAMILY DESERTION AT WIDNES —Before Mr F H Gossage and Mr II Gaskell, jun.. at Widnes Police Court, John Clark, a chemical labourer, was charged with desert- ing his wife and three children, aged respectively 9,7, and 11 years. On the 24th August Mr Scannell found the woman and children in a shocking condition in a house in High-street. lherq was no furniture in the place, and the occupants were nearly naked and without food. She stated that the prisoner had gone away the week previously, and taken his wages with him. He was in full work at the time. The woman and children were removed to the work- house, where they had since remained at a cost to the Union of .£l5 16s Bd. Every effort had since been made to find the prisoner, but it was discovered that he had gone to sea as a member of the crew of a Canard liner. He returned to his parents house in Runcorn for tne Christmas holidays, and was there apprehended on the previous night. Mr Scannell remarked that this was not the first time the pri- soner bad ran away from the town. Btie Bench sentenced the prisoner to a month's bard labour. THE SHIP CANAL,—The Accrington Co-operative Society have decided to take £l,OOO of Manchester Ship Canal shares. CATTLE DISEASE.—During last week 14 animals were attacked with swine fever in the townships of Appleton and Thelwall. Sheep scab has appeared on three farms in the townships of Lymm, Handley, and Warmingham, 28 animals being affected. ELECTION EXPENSES.—The return for the Widnes Division of South-West Lancashire was received at the Sheriff's offices, Preston, on Monday. The ex- penses of Mr. E. K. Muspratt are stated to be £719 17s Bcl. The expenses of Mr. T. C. Edwardes- Moss, M.P., in the recent election in the Widnes division, are returned at £770 19s. THE LATE BISHOP FRASER.—Mrs. Fraser has placed a memorial brass in the pavement at the centre of the new chancel of the Manchester Cathe- dral, with this inscription :—" In loving memory of James Fraser, D.D., 15 years Lord Bishop of Man- chester, this pavement, suggested by him four days before his death, is placed by his widow. Obit Oct. • 22, 1885. -Et 07." NEW MUSIC.—" To-day and To-morrow" is the title of a song just published by Messrs. Reed Brothers, London. It is composed by Mr. Henry Bond, Warrington; and it is very melodious, as his compositions usually are. The words are by an unknown writer; but they are, like the music, con- siderably above the average. The song is within easy range, and will therefore be tho more accept- able to the general public. The song is issued with. ad. lib. accompaniments for violin, flute or 'cello, which are in every way worthy of the original composition. CADISHBAD.—The annual Wesleyan tea meeting took place on New Year's Day, about 200 persons sitting down to tea. Afterwards the usual bazaar was held and over 400 persons were admitted. The stalls were well filled with useful articles of wear- ing apparel, ez,c., and there was a Christmas tree decorated with toys. The receipts, which are to- wards the debt on the Wesley Chapel, amounted to .f...3.s.—Sernions.—On Sunday night the Rev. Thos. Derry, the Wesleyan minister, preached a very stir- ring sermon to young men. On Sunday night the Rev. D. Clegg preached a sermon in the Congrega- tional Chapel on "The foe and the fight." The preacher dwelt on the temptations of the day and gave good advice to the young. BIRMINGHAM IRON AND STEEL WIRE TRADE.— The following, which we extract from "The Iron-A monger" of January 2nd, will be of. interest to many of our readers :—" The wiredrawing trade shares the depression of the Warrington wire in- dustry, which is still engaged in a life-and-death struggle with that of Westphalia, entailing heavy sacrifices both upon employers and employed. It is an open secret that the principal wire-drawing firms in this country are working at a loss, as the only alternative to closing their works permanently and suffering the trade to drift into the hands of foreigners ; but this state of things of course, can- not go on indefinitely, and either the cost of pro- duction will have to be reduced or the mills will have to be laid off till business and prices re- vive."

AN UNDESERVING DEBTOR. A man named George Watson, employed at Iloughton's wire works, Sankey Bridges, applied to his Honour Judge Ffoulkes, at the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, for an administration order. Appli- cant was questioned at length by a number of creditors as to his means and conduct, after which the Judge informed him that he had got into his present position by his own carelessness. ile (applicant) admitted that he was in the habit of drinking, and abusing his wife, whom he now blamed for the debts not having been paid. These orders were intended for debtors who were desirous of honestly discharging their liabilities, and he thought that Watson was not a fit subject to be granted an order. lie therefore refused the appli- cation.

CHESHIRE CHEESE.—The annual general meeting of the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture was held on Thursday at Crewe. A resolution was adopted in favour of the appointment of a Minister of Agri- culture. The secretary, Mr. Thomas Rigby, read a paper on "The best way of improving the quality of Cheshire-made cheese." He said one of the de- fects of a dairy of Cheshire cheese was the variety of quality, and he pointed out how great a gain it would be to the county if this could be remedied and a better average price secured. He urged the desirableness of establishing a school in the county where practical instruction in the art of cheesemak- mg could be given by competent teachers. The institution might develope into a superior school or agricultural educational establishment, where practical chemistry would be taubht and a scientific training gained. A COLLISION ON THE ROAD.—At Warrington County Court, on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes, William Gleave, farmer, of Burton- wood, sued Thomas Higgins, blacksmith, Legh- street, Earlestown, to recover the sum of £26 us, for damages to a mare, and loss sustained by him through the negligence of the defendant in driving a horse and trap on the New-road, Earlestown, on the 15th August last. The case had been adjourned from the last sitting of the court. Mr. P. Davies, solicitor, Warrington, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. H. L. Riley, solicitor, St. Helens, was for the defendant.—His Honour, during the hearing of the case, said that the evidence of a witness who had been called for the defence proved to his mind that there had been contributory negligence on the part of the plaintiff, but that the defendant might have aizoicled the accident. Therefore he thought that negligence rested with the defendant, and gave judgment against him for £l2 his.

_ THE GENERAL ELECTION AND DISESTABLISH- MENT.—The Liberator says :—" If the General Elec- tion has not done for the cause of religious equality all that was at one time anticipated, it is yet im- possible to doubt that a decided advance has been made towards its attainment, and that the Church Establishment has come out of the contest damaged and discredited to an extent that it has never been before. The net result of the election, in so far as we are concerned, is that it has sent to the House of Commons more than 230 members, who, in one form or another, are favourable to the policy of Disestablishment. Our strength in the new House will thus be at least double what it was in the last, although that was elected during the high tide of Liberal popularity throughout the country. The significance of this great.increase in the strength of the Disestablishment party in the House of Com- mons can be appreciated by everybody; and it fully explains the hesitation and reserve with which the supporters of the Establishment have referred to the election."
RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held on Thursday at the Town Hall, Waterloo-road. Present—Mr. R. Shaw, chairman ; Messrs. P. Speakman, S. Taylor, J. Pritchard, J.W. Light- burn, J. Dobson, H. J. Grice, W. Mellor, F. A. Lake, W. Fisher, W. Whittaker, Et. White, E. Imison, W. Farrell, T. Harris, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), E. Marshall (secre- tary), and M. Barker (surveyor). MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.—HOW SCARLET FEVER IS

In conclusion it is stated as an indication of the steps taken by the Health C.minittee to improve generally the sanitary condition of the town that for the six months from April Ist to September 30th 223 notices had been served for the abatement of nuisances, and in each case the nuisances had been abated. It was recommended by the committee that the Board authorise the connection of the High-street sewer and that of Devonshire-place as part of the scheme of sewer ventilation submitted by the medical officer of health. It was further recommended that a circular be sent to the Runcorn School Board and to the managers of tbe various schools diving an extract from the medical officer' leport relative to the child Walton, who was compelie-I to attend school during the peeling stage of scarlet fever. —ln moving the adoption of this report and minutes, Mr. Light- burn referred to the prevalence of cancer in the dis- trict, and remarked that it was necessary they should use every possible endeavour to stop anything calculated to propagate this dreadful disease. Scarlet fever had caused 25 per cent, of the deaths of the district, and the committee had written to the managers of schools and to the Schoool Board not to press children into school without exercieing great care. Though during the month Runcorn had the high death rate of 21 per 1,000 they were lower than that of the 12 largest towns.—Mr. Lake seconded the motion Mr. Pritchard, referring to the "Walton case " and the circular to be forwarded to the School Board, said the Board and the school visitors were extremely careful upon the sub- ject of driving children into school that had any infectious disease. But it was not on all occasions that they were able to ascertain what was the illness of the children. It would be an advantage if the school visitors could communicate the cases under their notice to the medical men.—The minutes were passed.

THE SCHOOL BOARD INCIDENT.—ATTACK UPON THE CHAIRMAN—LIVELY PROCEEDINGS. Mr. Lake read a paragraph relating to the locking of the Commissioners' board room against the School Board on the 12th December, which was reported in the Examiner, and asked whether it was correct ?—The Chairman : It is not correct.—Mr. Lake: if it is not correct there is an end of it. He ( Mr. Lake) said that the chairman of the Board quietly took upon himself to lock the doors of the board room against the School Board,. which seemed to him to be trespassing upon the province of the Finance Committee ? Mr. Fisher said he thought that it would only have been courteous to have allowed the Board the use of the room Mr. Lake, while admitting that the School Board had done wrong in not asking the permission of the Board to use the room, said they might hive taken the words of the chair- man, on a recent occasion, when be stated publicly that he saw no reason wby the echool Board should no; use the Commissioners' Board-room, in order to allow other roams to be used for the science-and art clas-es. as a sort of per- mission.—The Chairman observed that the Board could not grant the use of the rooms to any other body without the sanction of the Local Government Board.—Mr. Lake : That is quite true. Is it not a fact that the Board-room would have been unlocked that very morning but for your veto ? —The Chairman said that when the Beard entered upon the occupation of the premises the caretaker was ordered to keep all the rooms locked up, and no person could have entered the rooms except through the laxity of the official in charge. He said that he had ascertained that the care- taker had neglected the duty of locking the doors, and he gave instructions to have them locked as formerly.—ln reply to Mr. Lake, the Secretary said 1)4 application had ever been made to him by the clerk, or by any inern'oar of the School Board, for the use of the roems.—Mr. Lake said that the School Board were undoubtedly trespassers, and he thought that they had behaved disrespectfully to the Board; but wha,; he complained of was the school- boy trick of locking the doors against them, and watching the result.—Tbe Chairman said that the rooms had been locked fer a week prior to the meeting of the :.chotil Board. Do you think that the rooms should be left open? —Mr. Lake : Of course I don't. My contention is that you should have in-t-ucted our secretary to write to the clerk of the School Board that they could not have the rooms.—The Chairman : My view differs from yours to this extent—that I thought ttfe caretaker should do her duty.—Mr. Lake said if the Chairman did not really order the doers to be locked on account of the meeting of the School Board he would withdraw the remark to which the Chairman objected.—Mr. Lightburn said the proper way of acting would have been to have written to the clerk of the School Board, and not to have kept Canon Barclay waiting in the hall for ten minutes until the doors were unlocked.— The Chairman denied that any indignity was offered to any individual member of the School Board, and said his simple desire was to discharge his duty without knowing any- thing of the reasons why the School Board desired to take possession of the rooms.—After a further discussion of a rather heated character, the meeting came to an abrupt conclusion.

div.head: FATALITY ON RUNCORN BRIDGE.
div.p: THE FATALITY ON RUNCORN BRIDGE.

Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Bridge Hotel, Widnes, on Saturday, respecting the death of Martin Kato?, a steamship fireman, wliose muti- lated body WAS found on the Lonaon and North-Western Railway, near Runcorn Bridge, on Thursday morning. Mr. Ferrand, from the solicitor's department, Lime-street, represented the company. Evidence of identification was given by Catherine Mittan, 47, Seddon-road, Garston, with whom the deceased had lodged. He was about 30 vears of age.—Albert Tweedale, platelayer, who lodges at Cavendish- place. Greenway-road, described the finding of the body, and P.S. Robinson deposed to seatching the deceased's clothing, and he added that a telegram had been t eceived from the wife of the unfortunate man-45, High-street, Cannirg Town, London—stating that she was too noor to defray the cost of her bueband's burial. The officer added that on Wednesday night the driver of a train passing from Run- corn Bridge about the time that the deceased would pro- bably be upon it thought be went over something and pulled up, but was unable to make any discovery.—The Coroner said this ought to have been reported, and the driver present to give evidence.—Mr. Ferrand said that a guard had found a bundle which was thought to belong to the deceased in a comnartmenr, of one of the carriages com- posing the train in which he travelled.—The Coroner said they ought to know if there had been anybody in the same compartment with the defendant, because there were such things as being thrown out of a carriage. He thought the inquiry hart better be adjourned.— It transpired that the jury had concluded that the man was killed whilst walking down the line, and Mr. Ferrand was of opinion that the man had jumped from the train.—A juryman said there ought to be a watchman on Runcorn Bridge. If there had been one on the night in question probably the man's life would have been saved. A man might go on that bridge and never come off again.— The Coroner : You are speaking of the footpath. The Juryman : I am speaking of both the footpath and the line. —Another juryman : I have seen a case where a man got over the low wall and was lying helplessly on the line.— The Coroner : You cannot agitate that question here, but you can do so outside. A verdict to the effect that the de- ceased was killed by a passing train, rut that there was no evidence to show how he came on the line, was returned.— Mr. Atherton wished to draw the attention of Mr. Ferrand to the fact that several recommendations had been sent from juries to the L. and N. W. Railway Company, about a spot which was commonly said to belong to the firm of Gos- sage and Sons. Two deaths have occurred at that place through falling into the canal, and no protection had as yet been erected. He thought the suggestion of 12 inhabi- tants of Widnes ought to have some weight.—Mr. Ferrand said he had sent the suggestions to the railway company, but they would never recognise the place in question as a highroad.—Mr. Atherton remarked that the matter would have to be left in the hands of the ratepayers.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY

The monthly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse oh Tuesday. Br. Mclntyre presided, and there were present Revs. J. Lockwood and J. J. Bryant, Messrs. P. Speakman, E. Aaron, Warburton, Hadfield, Percival, Arrowsmi th, H. Linaker (clerk), and J. Adams (medical officer). THE ANOMALIES OF LOCAL GOVERNMENT. The Clerk said he saw from the newspapers last week that a Government Committee, of which Sir R. A. Cross was a member, bad been formed to draft a Local Govern- ment Bill. He took upon himself to write Sir R. A. Cross, who was vell acquainted with the Union, and placed before him the views of the Authority on sanitary rates. That morning he had received the following reply :—"Whitehall, 2nd January, 1886. Sir,—l am directed by the Secretary of State to acknowledge , the receipt of your letter of the 30th ult., urging. by direction of the Runcorn Rural Sani- tary Authority, with reference to the Local Government Bill, that the cost of the construction of works of a per- manent nature should be borne by the owners of property, and that the cost of maintenance only be borne by the oc- cupiers, and calling attention to cases of hardship under the existing Act.—l am, Sir, your obedient servant, E. LEIGH PEMBERTON."—The Clerk was thanked for his watchfulness and prompt action. INFECTIOUS DISEASES IN THE DISTRICT. Dr. Adams, the medical officer of health, presented a special report, in which he said another death frem scarlet • fever had taken place in Wood's-row, Halton-row, Halton, The case was the descendant of the death mentioned in his last report. He had again visited the locality and could find no new cases, while every precaution was being taken , and the premises, bedding, &c., had all been carefully disin- fected. There was another case of scarlet fever in Halton Village. The source of infection was believed to be Run- corn. The same disease bad also occurred at Moore. There was only one case, and ht bad that morning received notifi- cation of the death of the child. Infection was reported to have come frem Hatton, but he could hear of no cases in that locality. A case of diptheria had occurred at Keck- wick. As the patient had been exposed to direct infection elsewhere, they must regard the case as imported. Re- covery had taken place and no extension occurred. A death from typhoid fever bad occurred at Church-street, Prod- sham. The death return was the first intimation he had received of this case. An inspection of premisee, ittc., and disinfection should at once be made. The usual instructions were given.

MEDICAL OFFICER'S feIJARTERLY REPORT. The Medical Officer of Health reported that during the quarter ending December nst, 1885, the registrar's returna recorded 125 births and 78 deaths in the four registration sub-districts comprised in the Rural Sanitary District of the Runcorn Union. Of the births 58 were males and 67 fe- males; birth rate, 6•3 per 1,000 per quarter (or 25.2 per 1,000 per annum), against 131 births, with a birth rate of 0 0 per 1,000 per quarter (or 26.4 per 1,000 per annum) in the corresponding quarter of 1834. Of the deaths 44 were males and 34 females ; death rate 3.9 per 1,000 per quar- ter (or 150 per 1,000 per annum), against 87 deaths, with a death rate of 4.4 per 1,000 per Itaarter (or 17.6 per 1,000

per annum) in the corresponding quarter of 1884. Of the ' deaths 8 occurred in persons under 1 year, 7 occurred in persons between the ages of 1 and 5, 26 occurred between the ages of 5 and 60, and 37 in persons of 60 years and upwards. He was glad to state that zymotic diseases accounted for no more than four deaths viz., two from scar- let fever, one from whooping cough, and one from typhoid fever. The chief feature of the death rate during this quarter had been the very high mortality among persons of 60 years of age and upwards, no less than 37 out of the 7$ deaths, or 47.5 per cent of total deaths, having occurred in persons of 60 years and upwards. This report was considered very satisfactory, and Mr. Hadfield remarked that it was not true then that people in the Union were dying "like rotten sheep "through "ohmic gases," as stated at the last meeting. Dr. Adams: Who said that people were dying? The Clerk: Don't you read the Warrington papers? Dr. Adams: I didn't see that.
The Clerk : There was a very strong repnrt in the War- rington Examiner,

IV Adams: Did no one controvert thc statement. The Clerk: The Examiner rtcommended that a writ should be issued against a member of this Authority. Dr. Adams: The Examiner did? The Clerk: Oh, yes. Dr. Adams: Indeed. STOCKTON HEATH DRAINAGE.

Mr. Farrington, the inspector of nuisances, submittt.d an estimate of the probable cost of the turth,r improvement and cleansing of main sewers at Stockton Heath.—On the mo- tion of Mr. Warburton, seconded ny Mr. Aaron, it was de- cided to adjourn the matter until the end of the present quarter.

div.head: ISPREAD.-SEWER VENTLL&TION.
div.p: ISPREAD.-SEWER VENTLL&TION.

Dr. McDougall (the medical officer) reported that during the last month 31 deaths were registered. Of these 5 were due to scarlatina, 4 to dropsy following scarlatina, 2 to chronic bronchitis, 3 to cancer of various orgars, 3 to con- sumption, 1 to apoplexy, 2 to inflammation of the living membrane of the brain. 1 each to natural decay, eiarrhcea,

heart disease, epilepsy, and 3 to disease of uncertain origin. Of these deaths, 16 were amongst children tinder 10 years of age, and 2 were over 70 and under 80, and one was over eighty. The above thirtv-one deaths showed an average death rate for the 12 months of little Over 21 per 1,000 of the estimated population. The mother of one of the children whose death WAS reported as due to dropsy after scarlet fever made a statement on the 4th of January to the effect that her daughter, Martha Walton, aged five, was taken ill in November last, and remained in bed until Sunday, the 15th. On Monday the child went to school. No inquiry was made by the teacher as to the cause of her absence during the previous week. OP the Monday in question the School Board officer, Inglwfield, called and directed the mother to send the child to school. The child continued attending school for three weeks. On Friday, the 4th of December, it came home from school ill again. On the following Monday her elder sister, aged 8, attended at the school, but the teacher refused her admis- sion. On the same day the same school board officer called I again, and wanted to know the reason why they were not sent to school. Sbe told him that the eldest child had been

to school that day, but that the teacher refused her admis- sion. He then examined the sick child in bed, and felt at the lumps in her throat, and said she had only a cold, and instructed the mother to send the eldest child to school in

the morning, and the teacher was to be told that the child must go to school, and must be admitted, and that he (the school beard officer) said se ; and if she did not send her to school she would be summoned before the magistrates. She did not obey the directions of the officer, but on Tues- day took the child to a doctor, who said that it must have had scarlet fever, and was then suffering from dropsy. The child died on Sunday morning, the 13th of December last. The Medical Officer added that he would merely observe that the above was a plain unvarnished history of a truly sad case. This child, along with her elder sister, attended school dnring the period of the greatest activity of infection, and most probably her own death was hastened, if not entirely due, to exposure, during the peeling stage of the disease. On several occa- sions during the month repeated complaints were made to him of the continued suffering which some residents and occupants of business premises on the north and south sides of the lower portion of High-street bad had to endure owing to the continuation of the very offensive smells already re- ported. He drew the attention of the Authority to his last report, and he merely mentioned them now to remind the Authority that no serious step had been taken yet either to trace or ascertain the exact cause of the sudden generation of those highly noxious gases. It seemed to him that a better system of sewer ventilation than was already in ex- istence was urgently needed. There were now no fewer than six or seven trunk sewers of varying lengths convey- ing the sewage of the town to the river. Any sudden addi- tion to the normal quantity, and high tides banking up, the gas soon revealed its presence, should there happen to be faulty trapping, and as is feequently the case no trap at all to resist it. He had been making inquiry of Mr. Barker as to the distribution of these sewers aril their tributaries. He found that there would be no difficulty in connecting all the sewers of the tows into one system for ventilating pur- poses. Complaints had been made for many years of the nasty smells that one frequently encountered in Mongh- lands-lane, Greenway-road, and other parts of the town. It occurred to him that to establish a thoroughly workable system ef sewer ventilation, they must ventilate trite a rarefied medium at a high temperature, say of about 600 degrees. The waterworks chimney was admirably adapted for such a purpose, as it was considerably higher than the highest of their sewer reaches, and a subsidiary shaft might with advantage be connected with gas works chimney. The above scheme was necessarily imperfect, but he hoped that it would give the authority an outline of the network of sewers that had to be considered, as well as give them the ground work for the future development of an important sanitary improvement.—Mr. Lightbnrn observed that the suggestions of the medical officer had received some atten- tion already from the Health Committee, and should be de- veloped still further.—The report was referred to the Health Committee. THE CHAIRMAN AND HIS VETO.—HIS CONDUCT IMPEACHED.

The next business was the minutes of the Highway and Sanitary Committee. Mr. Taylor inquired of the Chairman why the minutes recommending the appointment of Mr. Wigg as a member of the Uoper Mersey Commission did not appear on the agenda P—The Chairman said the matter did not fall within the scope of the Highway and Sanitary Committee, and he gave instructions that the minute should be left out. As chairman of the Board, he strongly objected to its business being done in an unbusinesslike way. There had been no communication that a Vacancy had occurred— as far as the Board was concerned no vacancy had arisen— and therefore they could net have filled up a position which had not been vacated. There was only one way of doing business, and that was straightforwardly and above board, and in no hole and corner way. He did not want the Board to be in the absurd and foolish position of trying to fill a vacancy when none had arisen, and that was the reason he struck it out.—Mr. Taylor said the Law Clerk intimated to him that the vacancy had occurrred, and also informed him that it was the duty of the Highway and Sanitary Com- mittee to bring the matter before the Board. He did so, and a resolution was passed, and it was his opinion that it was not part of the Chair. men's duty to strike a minute out of the book when it was passed by the committee. (Hear, hear.)—The Chairman: Not even if it doesn't belong to the committee P—Mr. Taylor said the law clerk informed him the committee was in order.—The Law Clerk said Mr. Wigg told him that his appointment had expired by the effluxion of time. Next morning he told Mr. Taylor. and at the meeting of the committee he remarked that it had always been the practice hitherto for the committee to re- commend the filling up of this vacancy. Upon that Mr. Dobson made a recommendation that Mr. Wigg be re- appointed.—Mr. Lightburn said the proper coarse for the chairman to have adopted was to consult with the chairman of the Highway Committee.—Mr. (*rice agreed, and said it must be distinctly understood by the public that Mr. Taylor was absolved from any hole and corner work in the business. —Mr. Lake said the chairman had treated the Board in a drastic and, he thought, most impertinent manner by strik- ing out a minute passed by a committee composed of all the members of the Board. He (Mr. Shaw) presided over the Board, but had no powers of veto, and that was what Ka had quietly exercised there. He moved that the minute re- ferred to be inserted in the minutes.—Mr. Dobson said that if Mr. Shaw possessed the power of prevent- ing the minutes from appearing on the agenda paper it was a power that no other member had ever exercised be- fore.—The Chairman agreed with Mr. Dobson that no indi- vidual, no chairman of the Board, had the right to inter- , fere with any recommendation of a committee if the recom- mendation fell within its scope of business. He had made a remark about bole and corner work, and he would ask how did it arise that this thing should be done after the com- mittee bad separated. It was intended at that meeting to fill, or recommend that this vacancy should be filled up; and still a number of the members left the room, the chair- man amongst them, before the subject was ever hinted at. He had not been able to trace that in the past this vacancy had been tilled up by the Highway and Sanitary Committee, 1 and he should be very glad if Mr. Taylor would refer to the minutes for any such recommendation three years ago. He believed he was perfectly justified in the course he took. Hearsay was not business, and Mr. Taylor ought to have satisfied himself that there was a vacancy.—Mr. Lightburn : Don't you feel that the weak point in your position is that you set your judgment against the judg- ment of the whole Board as well as the Highway and Sani- tary Committee 2—The thairman : I have not had the judgment of the Board.—Mr. Lightburn : We have had that of the committee.—Mr. Taylor said he believed Mr. Shaw was the only member who had left the room when the business was brought forward, and stated he had to catch a train. Mr. Grice stated he had left the room. lithe standing orders were followed these mistakes could not occur.—Mr. Taylor then seconded Mr. Lake's motion.—The Chairman said if the Commis- sioners wanted to make themselves foolish fill up the vacancy.-.-Mr. Lake: It is not a question of foolishness but of your opinion.—The Chairman : It is no opinion I assure you.—Mr. Speakman supported Mr. Lake's proposi- tion on the ground that the chairman had no right to ex- ercise a veto.—After some further discussion the resolution was carried, and then, on the motion of Mr Dobson, secon- ded by Mr. Lake, the minute was referred back to the 1 committee.

• THE CANAL BOATS ACTS. The minutes of the Canal Boats Committee contained a report to the Local Government Board. It stated that during the past year 20 boats had been registered, making a total of 831 boats being registered at RULICOII3 since the passing of the principal Act. Sixty-nine cases of infringe- ment of the Acts had been dealt with. There had not been a case of infectious disease reported.—Mr. Lake moved, and Mr. Dobson seconded, the adoption of the report—Carried.

THE SANITARY CONDITION OF THE TOWN. In the minutes of the Health Committee was a reply to the Local Government Board's letter of July 23rd relative to Dr. Airy's letter. Alluding to the ventilation and flush- ing of the sewers being insufficient, the report pointed out that the majority of ttie sewers ran almost at right angles with the course of the river, and were of such a gradient as to render them self-cleansing. The contents were thus carried off before decomposition could take place. Some of the streets, however, ran parallel with the river. In one of these, Halton-road, ventilating grids and flushing pipes had recently been fixed. If these were found to be of ser- vice in ventilating tke sewer without being detrimental to the health of those living in the vicinity, it was intended to fix other ventilating grids in the streets requiring such ventilation. In another part of the town two archirnedian screw ventilators on iron shafts had been fixed. The Board at present had under consideration the feasibility of con- necting one of the main sewers with the high chimney of Messrs. flazlehurst and Sons' chemical manufactory.

div.head: DANGEROUS NUISANCE AT SUTTON.
div.p: DANGEROUS NUISANCE AT SUTTON.

The Inspector also reported that another cargo of cff.an- sive manure commonly known as saccharine had arrived at Sutton Turn Bridge Wharf. He had seen the material, which, if discharged, would cause a most abominable nuis- ance. On former occasions many parsons had bean seized with diarrhma, and even that morning the smell arising from the manure had caused sickness.—lt WAS resolved that the Inspector take immediate action against Mr. Rigby, the proprietor of the Wharf.

div.head: THR CANAL BOAT POPULATION.
div.p: THR CANAL BOAT POPULATION.

I Mr. J. Farringten read his anneal report of the action taken under the Canal Boars eels within the Runcorn Union. Durine the year periodical inspections had been made of canal boats nAssing threueb the district resul ing in the detection of 17 viola:ions er offences against the Acts. Proceedings were taken in 16 cases and 16 convic- tions obtained, the amount ef fiees and costs imposed being £ll 4s 61. It Was WI pleasure that he ' was able to vane that there Was a great and marked improvement disce,nible beth in the boats and boat population nhich paesed throueh the district, some of them being ecrueulously clean and might be taken with advantage as patterns by ccupiere of some dwellings which possessed far better Accommodation. Th • boats to which the foregoing rerrairks referred were thre:e which were " worked single," and tie might observe •hat amengst this class there is a general desiie to comply with the requisi- tions of the acts and regulariens. But three was much room for improvement in some of 11,e bare worked in pairs; the occupiers of these had an unfair advantage over those using single boats :s they could take a wheie family with them to reside rip•n the boats aid Borne of them (but there were exceptions) h .d no other residerce, but tbe soats and this class of the canal boat population could set the acts at defiance to a great extent and treat them with contempt. There was no doubt that at times much overcrowding exis- ted amongst :hero, and education was entirely neglected. In his opinion further powers were required to allow of more prompt act on being taken for offences committed by this class, and to render it imperative that the education of the children should be attended to.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
The monthly meeting was held yesterday at the Town Hall. Mr. Pritchard occupied the chair, and there were present Messrs. Lea, Handley, and Riglay (clerk).
MR. 13IISON-'S ELECTION.

The Clerk read a letter from the Education Department, from whick it appeared that owing to an informality in the election of Mr. Imison, it would be necessary to rescind the resolution of his election, and to again appoint a successor to Mr. Briscoe. It was decided to hold a special meeting for that purpose on the 19th inst.

THE " WALTON CASE." The Clerk said he had received a long letter from the Im- provement Commissioners with reference to the alleged treatment of a girl named Martha Walton.—Consideration was deferred. DENOMINATIONAL EDUCATION AND THE SCHOOL FEES. The Clerk said unfortunately he was unable to be present at the last meeting of the Board, as he was confined to home with an attack of bronchitis. At that meeting it was pas- sed that the fees at the new school should be at the rate of 2d per week for the mixed school, and girls school. and 3d for standard two and standard three, and 4d for standard four and upwards. He pointed out that that meeting was called for a special purpose, and the question of school fees could not be legally dealt with. An additional objec- tion was that the Education Department would net approve such a sliding scale.—Mr. Lea observed that the Board thought the fees were such as would not injure the schools for the coining half-year.— Übe Clerk : There is a distinct difference between schools which are built by the rates, and schools which are maintained by voluntary effort.— Mr. Handley : We shall be fining the people twice over if we charge a high fee.—Mr. Lea : 'I he fees are not as high as the Wesleyans.—Mr. Handley : But the intention of the Act is that we should make education as effi- cient and cheap as possible for the general body of ratepayers ; and we are met here I take it as a School Board representing the ratepayers.— Mr. Lee: It was thought by Father Fennelly. and I thought so too, that it would have a tendency to injure otlter scho.ds if tbe fees were much lower.—Mr. Handley said no member would have a desire to injure the denominational schools, but at the same time they ought to consider what would best promote the efficiency of the schools and the comfort of the people.—Mr. Lea thought the fees might be revised at the end of the half year.—The Clerk asked bow they were going to get over the objection of the. Education Depart- ment.—Mr. Lee said Canon Barclay was in favour of a threepenny fee, but his (Mr. Lea's) feeling was to put the school on the same footing as other schools as nearly as possible. The Wesleyans would feel it very much, as their fees were higher. Mr. Handley conten- ded that at the present time all the schools were full, and the new school had been built to accommodate the surplus childreefor which there was at present no room. Therefore the other schools could not be injured.—The Clerk asked was it not a fact that since the school visitors had driven the children into denominational schools, the managers of such schools had risen their fees from 33 to 53 per cent.—Mr. Handley proposed that the fees in the infant school should be 2d, and 3d in the girls' school.—Tne Chairman said although he was in favour of a threepenny rate, he would not like, in the absence of Canon Barclay and Father Fennelley, to rescind the resolution passed at the last meeting.—Eventually consideration of the subject was deferred until to-day at two o'clock.—The meet- ing then concluded. ,

div.head: FRODSIIA)I.
div.p: FRODSIIA)I.

KINGSLEY.—It is stated that the Rev. A. Griers, 8.A., who, it will be remembered, was appointed vicar of this 1 parish about twelve months ago, intends shortly to vacate the living of Ringsley for another appointment. PAROCHIAL CONCERT —A. large audience assembled in Frodsham Town Hall, on Wednesday evening, on the occa• sion of the annual parochial concert of the Parish Chnrcla A lengthy but excellent programme hael been provided, and all the vocalists met with an appreciative reception. There were several concerted pieces, and an enjoyable enter- tainment was given. SAVINGS BANIC.—The sixty-fourth annuli meeting of the trustees, treasurer, and managers of the above Institution was held in the TOWn Hall. Frodsham, on Tuesday, when Dr. Robinson presided. The Secretary (Mr. Pollard) read a statement of accounts for the year ended 20th November last. It was resolved that the statement as read be approved and adeoted. A vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. W. Hayes, treasurer, and also to Mr. W. H. -Pickering, for their exertions in promoting the best interests of the Institution. The thanks of the meeting were also given to the trustees, managers, and chairman. ANNUAL TREAT TO AGED PEOPLE AT FRODSHAM.—On New Year's Day Mr. Charles Linaker and family gave their second annual treat to the old men and women in receipt of parochial relief and residing in Frodsham or Frodsham Lordship. About fifty had been presented with a New Year's card during the previous week, each card containing a printed invitation requesting attendance at the Town Hall, Frodsham, to a tea party and concert. Thirty-seven per- sons put in an appearance. the remaining 13 being pre- vented from attending by infirmity or sickness. There was one old lady present who was in her 87th year. Roast beef, goose, bread and butter, tea, etc., were served out in a liberal manner, and the good things were partaken of most heartily.—The Vicar wished each a happy new year, and observed there was cause for thankfulness that God bad put into the hearts of people to strengthen the bonds of unity which should exist between the different classes, and which he was pleased to say was increasing throughout the country every year.—The tables baying been cleared, the guests were seated round the fire, and thoroughly ap- preciated and enjoyed the entertainment prepared for their amusement. The programme comprised songs by the Misses Riley, Miss Rigby, Mr. Holland, Mr. B. Rigby, Mr. C. Riley, Mr. J. Rigby, and Mr. W. Cameron. Mr. Linaker also gave two Lancashire readings, which were much appreciated. Mrs. Allsup gave a pianoforte solo and accompanied most of the songs. The proceedings were brought to a close about half-past eight by the singing of the rational Anthem. On leaving the room each person was presented with a packet of tea, a mince pie, an apple, and an orange.

CROFT BIIRULL SOCIETY.—The annual meeting of the above Society was held at the General Elliott Inn, Croft, when there was a large attendance of members. Messrs. Reginald Owen, jun., Charles Wild, and Peter Peters were re-elected trustees for the ensuing year ; Mr. Lewis Bircball, trea- surer ; and Mr. Alfred Dixon, collector and secretary. Mr. F. W. Ball and Mr. John Daintith were appointed auditors. The funds of the society amount to upwards of £B5O, and the number of members is 1,400. After the business had been transacted the members enjoyed themselves in dancing and singing until closing time; refreshments being provided by Mrs. Wild, the manageress. under the superintendence of Mr. Owen, jun., one of the trustees.

MR. BRUNNER,. M.P. AT GARSTONi On Thursday evening, Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.l) • for Northwich Division, presided at a gathering held in Garston Congregational Chapel, under the aus- pices of the Young Men's Society. In his opening address,

Mr. BRUNNER said he had bsen asked to come there by an old friend of his and by a good friend of theirs, Mr. James Handley. (Applause.) Wherever one went and wherever one read of such things, it was always the "young men's" society. When he was a young man he didn't like to be so exclusive—(hear, hear, and laughter)—and if the young men who were before him that night would take advice from him they would try to shake off a little of that exclusive feeling and try whether they could not gut young ladies ocea,ionally—(applause)—and he would advise them humbly to believe they wi,uld be all the better for it. That young men's society, he took it, was the outcome of a wish on the Rift of the young men to make their lives more round, more com- plete, and, he believed, more wholesome than was possible if they confined themselves merely to money grabbing, or if they combined the ordinary amusements with the effort to win their daily bread in an honest fashion. He found by the syllabus of the Cession recently come to an end that this effort on the part of the young men hat beets very worthily made. There had been one debate on what he might call a burning question, and he was very much pleased to hear that the conclusion to which that s ciety by a large majority had arrived was that free education was a noVe aim for us English people. (Applause.) He would close what he had to say by asking them to join with him in wishing with all their,hearts the eiladstones and the Brights of that society a happy new year an 4 prosperity. (Loud ap- pl iuse.)
A i.LEG: D AI:T 14.111 PT ED WIF MURDER
AT WARRINGTON.

At the Borough Court, yesterday morning, a man named Peter Leyland, who lives at Bank Quay, was brought up in custody charged with attempting to kill his wife, Martha Leyland, on the 2nd of Janu- ary. He was remanded for a week, the woman not yet being able to attend the Court.

On tile- previous Monday the prisoner was brolight before the magistrates and remanded, the case pre- ferred against him on that occasion being one of assault. From a statement then made by Chief Constable Hunt, it appeared that some years ago prisoner was convicted of ill-treating his wife. At that time be told the magistrates that the woman he had married had another husband living, and in consequence a prosecution for bigamy was institu- ted. Sentence, however, was not delivered against her. In the meantime prisoner went to live with another woman, with whom he parted, and after- wards resumed cohabitation with his wife. The Chief Constable received accounts of the prisoner's illusage of his wife, which brutality appeared to have cul- minated on Saturday night in a ferocious assault. In consequence of information received, Inspector Spinks went to the prisoner's house, and, after mak- ing inquiries, considered that it was a case that should be brought before the magistrates. Formal evidence was then given by a married woman named Williams, who said that on Saturday night prisoner kicked his wife in a brutal manner, inflict- ing serious internal injuries. Subsequently he wiped tip the blood which was on the floor, and went and told a police officer that his wife had had a fall. The injured woman was removed to the Infirmary, where she still remains.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. OCKLESHAW.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. OCKLESHAW.

Mr. Richard Ockleshaw, of Penketh, a gentleman greatly esteemed in the neighbourhood, died at his residence on Monday at the age of 85, he having been born on the 18th of April, 1800. The deceased gentleman in early life was a clerk in the Warring- ton branch office of the Manchester and Liverpool District Banking Company, and was subsequently one of the first district bank managers of the Man- chester and District Banking Company. He occu- pied that position at Stalybridge for about thirty years, but since 1865 had lived in retirement at Greystone House, Penketh. He was the possessor of considerable property in the locality in which he lived. He married Miss Brettargh, niece of Mr. Hall, of Ratcliffe, in 1852, but died without issue. His widow still survives him. The deceased gen- tleman never took an active part in politics, but was a regular and consistent supporter of the Church of England. He was of a very liberal dis- position towards the poor of the district. He had been ailing for a considerable time past, and, not- withstanding the careful attention of Dr. Spinks, he gradually grew weaker, and expired on Monday as previously stated. The remains of the deceased were interred yester- day in the burial ground attached to St. Mary's Church, Great Sankey. The body was enclosed in a lead shell, encased in polished oak with brass mountings, and the coffin bore the following in- scription on a brass plate :—" Richard Ockleshaw, born April 18th, 1800, died January 4th, 1886." The funeral cortege consisting of a hearse and six coaches, with private carriages, left the late resi- dence of the deceased shortly after half-past twelve. In the first carriage were the Rev. S. J. Jackson, I vicar of St. Mary's, Dr. Spinks, and Mr. E. W. Woods; 2nd, Mrs Ockleshaw, Mrs Nall, and M. William Crippin (nephew) ; 3rd, Mr. Henry Crip- pin, Mr. John Galloway (Manchester), Mr. Oswald Pike (Manchester) ; 4th, Mr. Wm. Sharp (bank manager, Liverpool), Mr. Charles Fairclough (South- port), and Mr. William Burton (Ashton-under- Lyne) ; sth, Mr. Walter Ashton (Rainhill), for- merly bank manager at Warrington, and Mr. Wm. Barlow (bank manager, Warrington) ; 6th, Mr. Wm. Wheeler- (Hall Nook, Penketh), and Mr. Robt. Lowe (agent to deceased's property.) The blinds of many cottages in the village were drawn until the funeral procession had passed. The scholars of Penketh schools formed a line for the cortege to pass through opposite the schools, the girls on one side and tke boys on the other. The burial service was performed by the Rev. E. J. Jackson, vicar. The i whole of the arrangements were left n the hands of Messrs. J. and W. Dutton, of Warrington; and Mr. J. T. Connor, of Sankey-street, supplied the hearse and mourning coaches.

THE PERILS OF A BAILIFF. • At the Warrington Borough Police Court on. Thursday the Mayor. (Alderman Harrison), acting as High Bailiff of the County Court, attended before the Bench and said that a man named James Dickenson had been arrested on a warrant charged with having committed a most brutal and cowardly assault on one of the bailiffs of the court, without any provocation. The man was totally unable to be present that morning, and he asked for a re- mand. Prisoner was then brought forward and charged with assaulting Joseph Waterhouse, county court bailiff, on the fifth of the present month. He was remanded until the following day. At the Borough Court, yesterday morning, Dickenson was charged with assaulting Joseph Waterhouse on the 5.h inst. • Mr. P. Davies, solicitor. Warrington, appeared to prosecute, and prisoner was represented by Mr. A. Brewne, solicitor, Warrington. The circumstances of the case, as detailed by Mr. Davies, were that on the day in question Waterhouse, acting in his capacity as bailiff of the Comity Court, wen to the house of the prisoner, 14, Philip-street, off Watkin- street, to execute a warrant in respect to a snalll debt. When he went to the house another bailiff named Tomas was already there. Prisoner's wife was in the house, and Waterhouse told her his business and produced his warrant. She went out for the purpose of obtaining the money, and returned in about half an hour. Soon afterwards prisoner came into the house, took off his coat, and asked the bailiffs what they were doing there, adding that he would have no bailiffs in his house. Waterhouse tried to pacify him, and said that he only wanted 103 2d, but prisoner said that they must go out, and took up the poker, which his wife tried to get from him. Some other women also tried to effect the same object, but he overpowered them, got hold of the bailiff, whom he pushed out of the house. Prisoner then, Mr. Davies said, delib.rately swung the poker round, and struck Waterhouse with it across the face, rendering him uncon- scious. Mr. Davies remarked that the bailiffs must be protected in the discharge of their duties, and asked for an exemplary sentence. Waterhouse, whose face bore evi- dent signs of Mileage, was then called and described the assault. His evidence was corroborated by the bailiff Thomas. Mr. Browne questioned the bailiff as to their conduct, and Thomas, in reply to the advocate's questions, denied that he had commenced the disturbance by using a stick. In defence, Mr. Browne said that his client was very much provoked at finding the bailiffs in the house and at Thomas striking him with a stick that he carried. PH- eoner, whe was at the time somewhat under the influence of drink, was greatly provoked. He then called a witness named Ann Simpkin, who alleged that Thomas hit prisoner with his stick and that prisoner then struck Waterhouse with his fist. She said that when she was present no poker was used, and was emphatic in saying that prisoner struck Thomas not with a poker, but with his fist. The Berela found prisoner guilty and imposed a fine of £5, including costs, or one month's imprisonment in default. On the ap- plication of Mr. Dar' 9 they decided to issue a warrant against Ann Simp' for perjury.

POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

- WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDA.Y.—Before Aldermen Burgess and Chandley. DEUNXENNESS.—Mary Coyne, who had been 22 times be- fore the magistrates, was fined 5s and costs for having been drunk in Buttermarket-street on Friday.—Thomas Garrity (19) whose 13th appearance it was, was sent to a gaol for a month for a similar offence. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Alder- man Davies, and Councillor Greening. MISCELLANEOUS —Ths. following were dealt with for drunkenness :—Jarnes Dewaine, in Queen-street, on the 24th ult, fined ss, including costs ; Brian Farriday, in Bridge-street, on Saturday night, fined 53 and costs ; Eliza- beth Parker, in Haydock-street, on the 24th ult, dismissed with a caution; William Yates, butcher's assistant, in the Market Hall, on the 26n nit, fined 103 and costs.—Harry Gorse, for driving a horse at a furious pace, in St. James's- street, Latchford, on the 24th nit, was fined 2a 6d and costs. —Matilda Carlisle was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Horsemarket-street, on Saturday night, and with assaulting a woman named Bridget INlcDonongh, whorls she struck in the face. She was discharged on premising to be of better behaviour.—John Longshavr, summoned for per- mitting a nuisance to exist on property belonging to him in Bostock-street. was ordered to abate the nuisance within a month, or be subj,ct to a penalty of 23 fid a day for every day that be neglected to carry out the order.—William Jones, forge labourer, was ordered to pay 13 a week towards the support of his stepson, who was at present in an In- dustrial School at Livs?rpool. Roustu GANG.—Edward Sauce (19) was brought up on a charge of bsing drunk and disorderly in Winwick- street. en Saturday night. Prisoner was described as belong- ing to a gang who would not work ; it was termed the Town Hill gang, and the members of it pounced on drunken men and robbed them. He was sent to prison for fourteen

days. TRANSFERS.—Tbe following transfers were granted:— The Old Crow Inn, Fennel-street, from Sarah BeliWo James Jolley; the Waggon and Horses, Butternsarket-street, from James Lvtbgee to Peter LyVigoe Speakman ; the Boar's Head, Town-hill, from William Newehall to John Derbyshire ; Green Dragon, Bridge-street, from John Nevins to Martha Horrocke ; Railway Inn, Bank Quay, from Kate Hartshorue to Samuel Hartshorne ; the Roan Cow, St. James-street, Latchford, from Mary Ann Hewitt to John Hewitt ' • premises in Fennel-street, from Wil- liam Holbrook to John Peers ; premises in Watkin-street, from Jane Lamb Edgew to William Jackson; the licence of 20, Claorley-street, from Thomas Forster Nevins to John Nevins; 60, Priestley-street. from George William Reynolds to Thomas Briggs. Tunsnwy.—Before Councillor Broadbent and Mr. E. J. Guest. A TROUBLESOME GlRL.—Mary Ellen Fearon, fustian cutter, was charged on a warrant with throwing stones on the 9th of October last, and with stealing, on the 19th Octo- ber, a shawl and a pair of clogs from the bouse of Francis Savory. Prisoner lodged at the house in question, and took away the articles, which belonged to a fellow lodger named Mary Baldwin. Oa the 9th October she was in company with some soldiers, absentees, who were ordered to barracks by a provo-sergeant. She followed, and threw stones at the sergeant. Prisoner was sent to gaol for a month. A DESERTER.—CbarIes Maxwell, a deserter from Her Majesty's 7th Battalion Cheshire Regiment, stationed at Chester, was remanded to await an escort. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Fairclough, Mr. R. Garnett, and Dr. Gornall. Ow THE ROAD.—Greorge Russell and Henry Lee were charged with being on the premises of the London and North-Western Railway with intent to commit a felony, on the previous night. A detective in the employ of the com- pany saw them in the goods-yard and took them into cus- tody. They informed the magistrates that they were tramping in search of work and had no felonious inten- tions. They simply went into the yard to find a place in which to spend the night.—The ease was dismissed. A VIGOROUS Assart.T.—Thomas Garvin, a young man, was charged with being drank and disorderly in Rylands- street on the previous evening and assaulting Mr. Weldon Watts, manager of "My Sweetheart" Company; he was also charged with assaulting P.C. Corbett and a soldier named Devine, who came to that officer's assistance. Pri- soner made a disturbance and fought with one of the door- keepers. He also used disgusting language and struck Mr. Watts. A cry of "police" was :aised, and Corbett got prisoner out of the hall and into Rylands-street. There be became very turbulent, and kicked the officer and the sol- dier who assistei hic.—A fine of 40s and costs, or in de- fault one month's imprisonment, wee imposed. THIIRSDAY.—Before Major Litton and Alderman Webstsr. MISCELLANEOUS.—A man named Carroll was fined Sc, in- cluding costs, for being drunk in irlam-street on the previ- ous evening.—William Irwin was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Rylande-street, and was tined ss, includ- ing costs.—Walter Sykes, for refusing to perform his task vgililst an inmate of the vagrant ward at the Workhouse was sent to prison for 14 days. THEFT BY a. GlRL.—Kate Powell (18), fustian cutter, was charged with stealing, on the let of January, a shawl, a handkerchief, and a het, value ss, from the house of Mar- tin Lynch, 15, School-brow. Prosecutris gave the girl a home for a few days, out of pity, and she returned the kindness by decamping with the articles. She was said to be an orphan, and the Bench took a lenient view of the case, simply recording a conviction against her on her prom- ise to go to the Workhouse.

WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY—Before Messrs. Bleckley and Tinsley. MISCELLANEOUS.—John Weston was fined 5s and costs for being drunk on the 14th ult at Poulton.--George i Green, for being drunk whilst n charge of a horse and cart on the 28th nit, and driving furiously on the Fearnhead. read, was fined lOs and costs.-Thomas Lannakin was fined 53 and costs for being drunk at Penketh.--Thomas Warburton was charged with allowing two horses to stray' at Burtonwood. The case was dismisd.--Nathap Taylor, for being drunk on tile licensed pr.Erniaes of Joseph Roberts, the Farmers' Aims, Poulton, on the 26th nit, was fined 5s and costs.
WIDNES POLICS COURT. MoNDLY.—Before Mr. J. Brock and Mr. 'l'. S. Timmis. Henry Dawson, James Murphy, John "'urn, Patrick Butler, Mary Dodd, and Michael Connelley were each fined for drunkenness.

The ice broke, and the boys were seen struggling in the water by some men, who were unable to reach the place in time to rescue them. The bodies of the lads were subsequently re- covered. AILA.amING RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—On Thursday evening the Great Eastern express for Norwich leaving London at five o'clock and an ordinary passenger train for Romford leaving three minutes later came into collision when nearing Manor Park station, six mites out of Loudon. The driver and fireman of the Ito:Ilford train and seven passengers were severely injured. Both lines were bloclced for several hours. STLRTLING DISCOVERY IN L STELMER'S FuRECASYLE.— About seven o'clock en Thursday morning a sailor on board the steamer Clanryre, lying in Maryport Dock, heard a strange noise, which induced him to ge to the lower fore- castle. He there found two seatnen—Stranney and Raton —in an unconscious state, and another seaman, John 31‘Lerey, was found dead. The unconscious men were car- Tied on deck, and restorativn appliA, nut they are in a very precarious condition. It seems that the men on retiring to bed early on Thursday morning took two bucketsfull or hot cinders with them to warm the place, and closed the door after them. 111'14-,rey 'Ong suffocated by the fames, and the other two men were only just discovered • in time. £100,000,000 in the COURT OFCHANCERY!—Cox in Co., 41. PRESCOT BOA RD OF GUARDIANS. LARGE DEFALCATIONS OF THE MISSING OVERSEER. The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held on Thursday, at the Boardroom, Whiston, near Prescot. Mr. John Leatherbarrow presided, and there were also present—the Revs. Thomas Chambers and J. Bar- nacle; Messrs. J. T. Hall, I'. Dobell, W. Tyrer, J. Fisher, W. Gerard, J. Lowe, W. G. Ashton, E. Syder, W. New- some, W. Swift, J. Ellison, T. Eatock, R. Tuson, Isaac F. Hill, J. Jackson, W. Birchen, P. Longton, and S. H. Hart- ley (clerk.) A letter was read from the Local Government Board, dated 24th December stating that they were in com- munication with the overseers for the Woolton district of the Prescot Union, relative to the proceedings of Mr. J. R. Wood, assistant overseer, who had suddenly left the dis- trict.—Rey. Thomas Chambers wanted to know if the Local Government Board were &log anything to ascertain the whereabouts of Mr. Wood. The Chairman replied that they were endeavouring to find out.—Mr. Chambers hoped the Local Government Board would find him. If they did not he thought the Guardians should try to do so.—Mr. Newsome asked if the clerk had any further information to give respecting Mr. Woods's accounta.—rhe Clerk said that an examination of the books was proceeding. He was not in a position to give the exact amount, but certainly the deficiencies were over £l,2oo.—Mr. Eatock asked if that amount was above Woods's security.—Mr. Hill replied that it was about £2OO above the security.—The Rev. T. Chambers urged that some stronger measures should be taken by the Local Government Board to prevent such scandals in the fature. Everybody was of opinion that something should be done, and much blame was being at- tached to the Guardians in this matter.—Mr. Kenwright said the Guardians appointed Wood. and not the overseers, 1 and they were to blame if anyone was. The overseers had no power to do anything in the matter. The Guar- dians were his masters, and not the overseers.—The Chair- man: The assistant overseer is bound to obey every legi- timate order of the overseers.—Mr. Hill : But they don't. —Rev. Thomas Chambers aeked when their were going to advertise for a successor.—The Clerk said the Local Gov- eminent Board would address a communication to Wood, and if he didn't reply a communication would be addressed to them as a Board, placing them in a position to elect a successor.—Mr. Newsome gave notice that at the•next meet- ing he would move that the rate of remuneration for the Woolton assistant overseer be 61 in the £ on the'amount of rate collected, instead of Vid, as at present.—Mr. Hill sec- onded. He said some of the overseers seemed to consider it a sinecure, so far as the out-districts were concerned. If that was so, he didn't see why they should par 71-d when other districts in the Union were paying 6d. -At any rate, that was enough until a man had proved himself worthy, whoever he might be.—The Rev. Thomas Chambers: 1 When may we expect a successor appointed ? The Clerk :. The Guardians will scarcely like to proceed to • till the office until the Local Gov- ernment Board have declared, it vacant. The Board will move Mr. Wood from his office, and then the Guardians can fill up the vacancy. It would not need a notice of motion for Mr. Newsome to move an alteration in the rate of re- muneration. He only need call the attention of the Guar- dians that be intended at the next meeting to move that 61 instead of 7-id be paid.—Mr. Newsome agreed to this course. He said he did not wish to say anything harsh, but after the remarks of Mr. Kenwright he felt justified on his own behalf and on behalf of other Guardians in resenting the statement. The Guardians were not to blame in the matter. The whole onus lay upon the overseers, and if they bad done their duty this would not have arisen.—Mr. Ken- wright said the overseers had not power to turn an assistant , overseer away.—Mr. Newsome fluid if they had not power they had power to keep a supervision over him.—The sub- ject then dropped, and the Board adjmuned.

Southampton-row, Lonoon.—Advt- SERIOUS COLLIERY ACCIDENT AT ASRTOS.—On Tuesday morning an accident of a serious character occurred at th'e , Mains Colliery of Messrs. Cross, Tetley, and Company, Bamfurlong, Ashton. The pit is one that is of a most diffi- cult character to work, owing to the gradients being of a very steep character. The tubs are drawn to the Ashton stage by means of a tail rope. and it appears that shortly after breakfast a train of twelve tubs was put on the shunt in order to be transferred to the landing stage. In the ordinary course the tubs were taken on, and when ascending the engine-brow, about nine o'clock, the bar coupling be- tween the first and second tubs in front suddenly smashed, and the eleven liberated tubs ran rapidly down the brow into the empty road, where they. came in contact with other tubs. Five' drawers were near the spot at the time, and all of them were injured. Wm. Painter, of Ashton, had his thigh broken, and Robert Roberts, of the same Place, was internally crushed. The other three, Edward Percy, Crippin'e Lump, Ashton; William Roberts and J. Macdonold, Ashton, were only slightly injured. As soon as the accident had taken place the attention of Mr. .Top- ping, the manager, was directed to it, and with the aid of Mr. John Rothwell, the underlooker, and Mr. John Hilton, head fireman, the injured men were conveyed to the stir- facts, and subsequently to their own homes. There is a large staff at the colliery in connection with the St. John Ambulance Association, and these rendered first aid where- ever it was required. Several of the injured were seen by Dr. Hannah, and others by Dr. Mapei, and it was thought best in Painter's case to remove him to the Infirmary, li:hither he has been conveyed. Percy, it may be men- tioned, only started work that morning. Lif(fresni ed ExtnL; Postage d. WE MYSTERIOUS DROWNING AT WARRINGTON.

On Saturday afternoon an inquest was held at the Black Bear Inn, Latchford. by Mr. Blunt, deputy coroner, on the body of the man found in the Mersey on the previous day. The proceedings were watched on behalf of the police by Inspeotors Berry and Spinks. John Ward, a labourer, living at Bolliugton. near Altrineharn, said he had a brother named Michael Ward, who was also a farm labourer, and lately lived at the same plane. He was unoaarried, and about 27 years of age. He had, not seen his brother since Saturday. October 10,h, when he was at Bollington about five o'clock in the afternoon. IDeceased told him he was going to Warrington, and he had not seen him since. On Sunday afternoon he was told by another farm labourer named john Byrne that his brother had had a row at Warringtoa between twelve and one o'clock, with John Scaulon, Thomas Scanlon, and others. He had seen the body of the deceased, and recognised it as that of his Ibrother Michael Ward. He recognised it by his I boots, his clothes, and by a broken tooth. Byrne told him (witness) that he had last seen his brother after the row with the Scanlons running up Arp The cap produced was the one deceased was wearing on the Saturday in question.—ln answer to the jury Inspector Spinks said that the cap had been fone4 near the Arpley railway bridge.—Mary Sockett, wire of James Sockett, living at 9, Arpley-walk, said that about ten minutes past twelve o'clock on the night of Saturday, the 10th Oetober, she was standing at her front door, and heard some one shout. he went out of the house by the back door and about, thirty yards distant she saw eight or ten men who appeared to be quarrelling. She saw John Scanlon and his father there, and they were talking in a very angry tone in Irish to the deceased. She went away, and on returning saw the deceased coming past Mr. Mullin's back door. He appeared to have been badly beaten, and stooped down to pick something up. She thought it was his jacket. She went to the top of the walk, where she saw the Scallions and Byrne, and she said " Ward has done nothing wrong that he should be beaten." Byrne asked witness which way Ward had gone, and she told him in the presence of the Scanlons. She also asked the men to go after Ward, as he would very likely get drowned or be locked up. It was a very dark night. She did not sea either of the Scanlons running after the deceased. By a Jury- man : The men would hear what I said, but they made no reply.—Charles Foster, labourer, Woolstoa, deposed to finding the body floating in the river on the previous Friday morning at Latchford weir. The body was very much decomposed. Sergeant Cox said that on receiving information of the discovery of the body he and P.C. Smith searched the clothes of deceased, and found 78 7d in money and a knife The body was too far decomposed to ascertain. whether there were any marks of violence upon it.— Inspector Spinks mentioned that after the Warring- ton police had received information of the disappear- ance of deceased the younger Scanlon was arrested on suspicion of having caused his death. The older Scanlon disappeared after his eons arrest, and ultimately the prisoner was discharged on his own recognisances to appear when called upon. 'The borough police had made inquiries, and they had got evidence to show that neither of the Scanlons fol- lowed the deceased, but that they went to their lodgings almost immediately after the row. He might say that the Chief Constable was perfectly satisfied that the Scanlons had nothing to do with the death of the man.—The Coroner thought it was advisable to adjourn the inquest in order that John Byrne, who is in Ireland, might be present.—The inquest was then adjourned till Monday.
