WARRINGTON BLITE4.I COAT BROTHERLY SOCIETY. The thirty-first annual dinner of this society was held at the Lion Hetet, on Monday evening. The chair was occu- pied by Mr. J. C. Parr, who was supported by the Mayor of Warriterton (Aldermen Harrison), Aldermen navies and eb,ter, Capta+ns Reynolds sod Nicholson, the Rev. E. C. B. Carleton, Messrs. R Davies, H. B. Weite, Tnns. Morris, Wm. Owen, J. Adams, F. Monks, T. Robinson. P. Davies, E Rose (head master of the Blue Coat School), W. J. For- shaw (hon. sec.), John Allen, J. Dewhurst, R. Anderton, T. Line, W. H. Bowes, Loieglands, F. Rose, W. S. Burgess, J. A. Snort, J. I,laiees, T. Whittaker, I'. Artustronet, J. Hewitt, F. Tamer, Ed. Smith, W. Holbrook, Joseph Sykes, Slater, Thomas Hill, A. Rathbone, J. Povev, John Ashton, T. Banks, J. H. Deelev, T. E. Hughes, C. C. Bowes, George Weave, J. W. Pritceard, P. Morris, W. Wilcock, W. 13robbin, F. Short, T. Pilling, A. Deelev, W. Pratt, and F. A. Dealev. Letters regretting not being able to attend the dinner had been received from Lord Winmarleigh and Colonel Ireland Blackhurnc. A bountiful repast having been served, and the tables cleared, the usual loyal toasts were given from the Chair, and beh were acknowledged with musical hervoue.. Mr. FORSIIAW (hon. sec.) then read the 31st annual report of the society, in welch the committee acknowledged the support received. The benefits conferred by the society, al- though comparatively unseen, were sensibly felt by many a poor and unpretected orphan. The committee wished to iernied submcribers that the society was formed mainly with the aj-cts of visiting children when they left the Blue Co Institution with a view of obtaining them situations, to take all active interest in their welfare, and by means of the influence gained over them to endeavour to direct them in the right path, to make grants of clothes and money to poor boys, and to encourage their regular attendance at public woi-ship. Tnese objects the committee had en- deavoured to carry out, and it was believed that their efforts had been so far successful and were generally appreciated. The committee were much encouraged from time to time by assurances from old Blues of their continued interest in the society. The financial position of the society was most satisfactory. The committee had spent £43 183 in clothes and grants during the past yen-. and, after satisfying all claims, tbere was a balance of £B4 Ss 3d standing to the ceedit of the society. They would be glad to lessen that balance if by so doing they could further the usefulness of the society. The committee begged to offer their warmest thanks to the trustees of the Blue Coat School, and their other patrons and friends, for their valuable and constant support, and •ook toe opportunity of wishinee all present a Happy New Year. (Applause.) Alderman PICKAIRRE proposed "The Church," coupling with it the "Bishop and clergy of the diocese and minis- ters of all denominations." Our dear old church, he said, was a refnge for the poor and a consolation for those who were in affliction or sorrow. Its doors were always open for anyone who desired to enter. He hoped that would always remain so and that the old Church of England, notwithstanding he assault she had had, was still destined to show that her foundation was on a rock and that she could not be thrown down with impunity. The bishops and clergy, with very few exceptions, endeavoured to bene- fit society as much as possible and bring people up in just fear of the Lord. Having referred to the deaths of the Bishop of Manchester and Dean Howson he coupled with the toast the name of the Rev. E C. E. Carleton.—The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON, responding, referred to the so-called attacks upon the church. He thought they might con- gratulate themselves on the way in which they had got through the crisis, and he might say that on the whole the results had not been unsatisfactory to the church. It WAS rather curious to observe,that no sooner had those attacks been begun than those who commenced them, feeling alarmed at the feeling thy had raised, immediately sought to allay that alarm by giving all possible assurances that they did not mean it, and that it was only their fun. But without estimating the value of those assurances he thought they ware very gratifying as bearing testimony to the pub- lic feeling that set in in favour of the church. (Hear, hear.) As to them he did not think churchmen need have great apprehensions. The church had weathered many a worm, and survived many an assault, from the days of Nero downwards, and he thought that statesmen would take care not to overrate their powers, because the church was after all a spiritual body, and that fact itself limited the powers of a stateman's interference. Real statesmen would feel that it was to their advantage to be friendly towards the church rather than antagonistic. It was always, and always should be, he took it,. the function of religion to be favourable to civil government, and to inculcate those sen- timents and principles which were helpful to a statesman, and he thought they had done that somewhat in the church, teaching humility and due submission to authority, teach- ing people, in those time-honoured and well-known words, to " honour and obey the Queen and all that are pat in authority under her." When it was borne in mind that such was the mission of the church, it was the duty of a statesman to support such an institution, and it was at their peril if at any time they ventured to alienate an institution of that kind, or if they sought to dispense with the ale which it was in her.power to give. They churchmen had sought as far as they could to make religion natural, and to present a christian religion to the nation which all might receive. They had thought that It would be a good thing to unite the whole religious profession. That was an ob- ject which he conceived was certainly worthy of the church. It was one they were not ashamed of, and if they had failed, though some fault might be at the door of the church, much of the fault lay at the door of her opponents. He did not think it would be much consolation to them to , know that they had done what they could to render such a consummation entirely impossible. He then spoke of church reform. Mr. T. Lane then played a pianoforte solo. Mr. ROBERT Dams gave " The army' navy, and reserve forces." War, he remarked, had indeed become a game of science as much as brute skill and courage, but at the same time they must feel that the spirit that carried their. fore- fathers through so many trials and enabled them to meet the great Armada without terror or apprehension bad not yet died out.—Captain NIOHOLSON acknowledged the compli- ment. Lord Wolseley, he said, speaking the other day, commented on the fact that in England the army and those connected with it formed a very considerable portion of the nation. In former days there was oily a small standing army and, except in time of feared invasions, little was thought of the army. Now about one million of her Majesty's subjects were engaged either in the army, navy, reserve, or some other department. Mr. Percy Davies sang a song, which was encored. The second song that he gave in response was as loudly ap- plauded as the first. Mr. FORSILAW proposed "The trustees of the Blue Coat School." They knew the trustees to be gentlemen of the highest character, who were associated with every philan- thropic and useful object in the town, and some of whom fulfilled important public duties. But he had to speak of them as trustees of that noble institution the Blue Coat school. He said noble because it had done, and was doing, a noble work, and Warrington had every reason to be proud of it. The trusts of the school were being admini- stered wisely and honestly for those for whom it was founded. The trustees and the head master took care that the educa- tion given in the school should he based upon true religious principles. He hoped that those principles would never be surrendered, for it was absolutely necessory that religion should be connected with education. Were they to attend at the service which was given in the chapel on Sunday evenings, they would find that thorough religious instruc- tion was implanted in the minds of the Blues, and that the services were very impressive. The standard of education at the school was high, and if the Blues wished to compete with others they must keep up their education, bestir them- selves, and be up and doing. Nothing would more please the trustees than to know that the Blues were making good use of the education that they had received at the school, and were endeavouring not only to be a credit and honour to the institution, bat to the town. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. BURGESS supported the toast. He endorsed what Mr. For- shaw had said with regard to the education given at the school.—The Cuetnatax, in response, said it was very gratifying to the trustees to feel that those who had been educated in the school entertained such feelings as had just been expressed. It was creditable alike to the trustees, the master and mistress who had conscientiously and ably conducted the school, and to the Blues themselves, for it showed that all had been working for the advancement and good of the institution, and that they had achieved the suc- cess that they deserved. Speaking of success reminded him of two very signal inetances. Mr. Forshaw, he understood, had recently passed the preliminary law examination to qualify as a solicitor, and would soon join that responsible and honourable body. (Applause.) The second instance was that of Mr. Lane, who had risen to be usher in the eshool and had just gained a free scholarship in the London Conservatoire of Music, and had also been appointed assis- tant organist at St. Barnabas Church in London. (Ap- plause.) These, among other instances, were very gratify- ing to the trustees and must be very satisfactory to the master and mistress, to'whose care and good teaching they were mainly attributable. He fully concurred' in the neces• sity for having religious training combined with education, , and—mhde believed e rmanD saoc t r espan otherwiseded . was a They s d considerable satisfaction in the knowledge that the school, notwithstanding the competition everywhere around, still holds its ground, and that the lads who left it seemed to be progressing and achieving positions in life creditable to the school and themselves. He believed that was greatly brought about by religion being attached to the education given them. Mr. E. Rose sang 'The Union Jack of Liberty." Mr. PERCIVAL gave the "Mayor and Corporation of War- rington, and the town and trade of Warrington." He re- ferred to Aldermen Harrison having been thrice elected Mayor as evidencing the confidence that was reposed in him by the burgesses. The members of the Corporation all did their best to bring about improvements, and they saw im- provements on every hand. Trade was now depressed, but he hpped that they would soon rejoice in better times.—The mexon (Alderman Harrison) acknowledged the honour, and remarked that the Corporation as such could not hope to avoid criticism, but honest criticism he regarded as the very salt of official life. As the governing body in War- rington they must take the responsibility of that position. Were men mere machines both imperial andlocal govern- ment would be as easy as playing a game of chess. But men were not mere machines, without sympathies, feelings, and prejudices, which al' had to be taken into account, and they could not hope suc- cessfully to govern unless they could take them into account. He believed that from the time Warrington was incorporated they had progressed in a most satisfactory manner. They

TERRIBLE TRAGEDY IN IRELAND.—A terrible tragedy is reported from Amthamullen, near Newtovrnbutler, county Fermanagh. On Saturday morning, about nine o'clock, while a man named Crozier, a small farmer, was seated at breakfast with his wife and ten children--the eldest a young man of 20, and the youngest an infant—Crozier called his wife an ugly name. She anied the aspersion, and dared him to prove it. He then lifted a knife, with which he had been cutting bread, and attempted to strike her with it, but the eldest son interfered, saying he would not allow him to strike his mother. Crozier then ordered his son to leave the house and not return to it. He went out, and was immediately followed by his mother, who stood about three yards from the door. The second son (Jeremiah), seeing the barrel of a gun protruding just outside the door, called out to his mother, and she had Net 'turned round to ascer- tain the cause of the alarm, when the gudwas discharged, and the bullet struck her in the mouth, and she fell dead on the spot. The terrified children carried the body into the house, a work in which they were assisted by Crozier, who aopeared to be suddenly stricken with deep remorse. When the body was got inside, Crozier attempted to cut his throat with a razor, but was prevented. He then laid hold of the gun, and took it outside and smashed it on the pavement. Information was given to the police, and Crozier was imme- diately taken into custody. A 'FIGHT BECTWAHN COLLIHRS.—At the Presoot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Mr. F. W. Earle and Mr. A. R. Gladstone, Thomas Molyneux and James Swift, colliers. were summoned for committing a breach of the peace by fighting together at Prescot on the 20th December. Both defendants pleaded guilty.—They were each bound over to keep the peace for three months, themselves in sureties uf , £lO and two suteties of 5.5 each.

_ Gears TRBSPASS —Robert Jones and Samuel Jones, col- liers, living at Huyton Quarry, were summoned at the Pres- cot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Messrs. F. W. Earle and A. R. Gladstone, for trespassing in pursuit of game on land at Tarbock, occupied by Joseph Watkin, and belong- ing to the Earl of Sefton. • The prosecution was c'onduc- ted by Mr. J. 0 Swift. The defendants pleaded guilty.— The chairman remarked that if they had not given wrong namts and addresses they would probably have got off easier. Each would be fine.l 20s and costs, or one month's imprisonment. SINGULAR CHARGB.—A somewhat singular charge of theft was heard at the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday, before Messrs. F. W. Earle and A. R. dladstone. John James Tipton, 15 years of age, was charged with stealing 9s 6d, the property of Sarah Feeney, a school teacher at Orrell. Superintendent Barker stated that on the 24th December Miss Feeney arrived at Preecot station by train, and the prisoner offered to carry her parcel to the village. She allowed him to do so, and afterwards gave him what she thought was sixpence to get changed. intending to give him Sd. Unfortunately, what she thought to be a sixpence was a half sovereign. The boy went to a shop, and was given change for half a sovereign. but he only handed six- pence to the prosecutrix. She gave him threepence, and a short time after he had gone she found that she had given a halt sovereign instead of a sixpence. She gave informa- tion to the police, and the prisoner was apprehended. He admitted having kept the Os 6d out of the half sovereign, and said he had since spent it. He was committed to prison for 14 days with hard labour. Passcur LOCAL BOARD—The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday evening; present: Messrs. J. T. Hall (in the I chair), T. S. Preston, J. Dennett, H. Makin, W. Hatton, H. Whitfield, W. Goldreorth (surveyor), H. Cross (clerk), and Dickenson (inspector).—Telephone Poles: The Clerk re- ported that the Lancashire and Cheshire Telephone change Company were prepared to nay is per year for each pole erected in the township, and it was decided to accept that sum so long as only one wire was affixed to the poles. —Financial Items: The collector reported that since the last meeting he had collected £74 us id of the rate made on the 4th November, and he had deposited that sum with the treasurer. The minutes of the Finance Committee stated that the clerk had submitted 13 tenders for loans, and it was decided to borrow £2,000 for three years, at four per cent. interest, in order to repay a loan from Messrs. Hesketh and Higson, upon which 4i per cent. interest was being paid. The followiag tenders were accepted :—Mr. Bixter £3OO, Mr. Rhodes Fazakerly £2OO, Mr. Joseph Haigh £5OO, Mr. Henry Makin £3OO and £5OO, Mr. William Ashcroft £2OO. On the motion of Mr. Preston, seconded by Mr. Hatton, the salary of Mr. Bixter (collector) was increased from £2B to £3B per annum. Mr. Whitfield voted against the proposal. A letter was read from the Local Government Board in reference to the balance of a loan of £7OO obtained in 1876, and the whole of which, it was reported by Mr. Hazlehurst, the district auditor, had not been spent. The Clerk explained that the balance was in the Treasurer's hands, and was bringing in interest. The loan was obtained to carry out drainage works and what was left would have to be returned. The letter was re- ferred to the Finance Committee.—Births and Deaths : Mr. Fogg (registrar) reported that during November the deaths were—Prescot 7, corresponding month last year 8, Eccles- ton 2, last year 1; death rate (both periods) 16.82 per 1,000 of the population. The births were 12, against 15. In•the month of December the deaths were—Prescot 17, Eccles- ton 1; last year Prescot 11, Eccleston 4 : death rate 3365, last year 27.42. The births. were 27, last year 23.—Mr. Whitfield drew attention to deaths from bronchitis, and sug- gested sanitary arrangements with respect to middens, &c. —This was the whole of the business.

div.head: PRESCOT HIGHWAY BOARD.
div.p: PRESCOT HIGHWAY BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday, Mr. W. L. Evans presiding. There were also present—Captain Willis, Messrs. J. Leatherbarrow, J. Lowe, R. Tyrer, H. Cross (clerk), W. Goldeworth (surveyor). and W. Goldaworth, our. (assistant surveyor). STANS-I.4llM—ln reference to the improvements in Stank-lane the Surveyor reprted that he and Captain Wil- lis had met in Stank-lane with the view of considering its improvement. Captain Willis was wishful that a portion at a time should be done as the funds would not allow of the whole of it. A portion where there was a •considerable amount of traffic from the collieries was very narrow and there was no footpath. It was possible that piece would be the first submitted for their consideration. TELEPHONE AND TELEGRAPH WIRES...—. The Surveyor said he had had an application from the Telephone Com- pany to erect several poles for the extension of the tele- phone wires for the use of the county constabulary, in Sandy-lane' south of the workhouse. Narrow-lane, and St. James's-road. He did not think there could be any objec- tion. The Board decided to leave the matter in his hands. —The Chairman drew attention to a pole erected opposite the alms houses in Warrington-road, and which, he said, was very objectionable.—The Surveyor said the pole in ques- tion was a telegraph pole and had been erected by the postal telegraph officals. He had several times ordered poles to . be put further back, and be had given instructions that no more were to be put down without his consent. He had written on the subject, and the manager had replied that he was under the impres- sion Mr. Goldsworth had given consent for the pole to be erected, but he would see to the matter.—Mr. Leatberbarrow asked if they had any power over the poles. Could the Government place them where they liked ?—The Clerk : No; they must have our consent.—Mr. Leatherbarrow said a man recently walked against the pole, and ha had to be carried home insensible. The pole had been painted white, but it could not be seen on dark nights, as there were no lamps about.—On the motion of Mr. Leatherbarrow, seconded by Mr. Tyrer, it was • resolved that notice be given to the Postmaster General that unless the pole be removed within 11 days the Board would remove it and charge him with the cost. THE NNW RAILWAY.—The Surveyor submitted a plan of a proposed new railway running through the district and crossing the highways. The railway started from St. Helens at the back of the Town Hall, came through Windle and a portion of Ecclestan. The first road in their district that it interfered with was at Eccleston Platt, and in that case the road was taised 18 f.:et 6 inches. The next cross- ing was close by the, Knoweley Waterworks, and it was pro- posed to deviate the road. The line then came on to high- way leading from Knowsley straight into Kirby, and the road was lowered 5 feet At Knowsley the road was lowered 1 foot. He thought they should have some formal agree- ment with the company as to the repair of the bridges and roadways.—The clerk was instructed to draw up the sug- gested agreement. THE BOARD AND ST. HELENS CORPORATION.—The Clerk read a letter he hael addressed to the Town Clerk of St. Helens with reference to the heavy traffic occasioned by the Corporation carts in consequence of the works at the Knowsley Waterworks. He remarkyd that he had received no reply. EXPENDITURE.—The Surveyor reported that the expen- diture during the five weeks ending 31st December was as follows :—Bold, £23 18s lid ; Knowsley, £l6 16A 10d ; Rainhill, £22 16s lid ; Whiston. £l3 13s id; team labour, £35 44 6d ; new materials, £3l 7s 6d ; inci- dentals, £2 19s 7d; total, £146 17s 4d.—This was the principal business. .

The Lord Lieutenancy of Devonshire has been conferred upon the Earl of Iddesleigh. Dr. t'alinon, Reius Professor of Divinity in Dublin Uni- versity, is mentioned as a probable candidate for the vacant Primacy. The Rev. J. Watson, rectir of Orton, Longneville, has died from injuries received to the leg while kneeling at prayer. • EARLESTOWN GOSPEL MISSION. A treat to the children connected with the Gospel Mission was given in the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, on New Year's Day. About 200 children wore regaled with a substantial tea, sandwiches, &c., the arrangements for which were carried out by Messrs. G. Birks, Dickens, H. J. Darman, Killender, Eachus, Gee, Jameson, &c. Mr. Dickens afterwards ad- dressed a few seasonable words to the children, who spent the evening in various games.

- Ann Sowster, widow, of London, while walking with her brother along the line from Kilsby Station, near Rugby, to Ilillmorton, on Saturday, was knocked down by the eleven o'clock express from Euston and instantly killed, her body being fearfully mangled.

div.head: SCIENCE, ART, &C-
div.p: SCIENCE, ART, &C-

The sixth comet of the present year is announced to have been discovered by Mn.i Brooks, of Phelps, New York. The date of discovery is not given, but it was observed at the Harvard College Observatory on Dec. 27, at 811. 12m. p.m., the position at that time being—R.A. 19h. 55m. 405.; N.P.D. 85degs. 52m.; daily motion in RA., + urn.; in N.P.D.-28. IMPORTANT INVENTION IN LIGHTING.—From Vienna is reported an invention which will, it is said, by some light engineers, completely rev'olutionise the present system of gas lighting. The invention has just been perfected in the chemical labatory of the Vienna University. It consists in rendering a cotton wick incombustible by im- pregnating it with a metallic liquid. Thus treated, the wick, instead of burning, merely glows, emitting a radi- ance not unlike that of the electric light The whole pro- cess is very simple, and the great advantage of the inven- tion is that it may be applied to any gas burner. A PRECIOUS QUARTET.—A correspondent states that a wealthy person who was devoted to music died lately in Paris leaving behind four stringed instruments, all made by Stradivarius, which could with difficulty be matched. One violin, dated 1737, the year of the maker's death, was his last work, and was named by Stradivarius the "Swan's song." Its owner paid 17,000 francs for it. A second violin, 'dated 1704, was purchased for 12,750 , francs. The viola, dated 1728, was bought for 19,000 [francs. And for the violoncello, made in 1696, the owner paid 17,500 francs. Duly authenticated documents attest the origin of each instrument. SPHERICAL MIRRORS FOR SOLAR SIGNAELING.—The panoramic mirrors or silvered balls frequently seen in gardens are advocated by Mr. Hatt, in a note to the French Academy of Sciences, for heliographic purposes in preference to plane mirrors. Their advantage lies in the greater intensity of the luminous point, which can therefore be seen to greater distances.*From experi- ments made by him during the past summer, he found that with a sphere of small diameter the image per- ceived at 15 kilometres with a lunette had a splendour comparable to that of a star of the second magnitude in a field feebly lighted. Such an image, which can be pro- duced at little expense, would, he thinks, be useful in topographical triangulation.—Enyineeriny. STEALING ELECTRICITY.—The leakage to the earth of Ithe underground leads of the Edison electric lighting system, from the central lighting station in New York, U.S., is said to be about three amperes, the tension being 110 volts. It was found that numerous unprincipled persons had availed themselves of the opportunity to steal electsicity—an offence surely unknown to statute law—and use it for operating motors, and for induction coils. The method of filching the electricity was by I boring through the iron pipe surrounding the insulating I compound, and then further into one of the copper 1 leads; a set screw fixed into this orifice, formed one connection and the earth the other. Of course this ! connection was made beyond the electric meter. It was hardly worth while to maintain the continuous espionage necessary to detect and punish these pilferers; but the superintendent of the station, Mr. Chamberlain, coupled I in extra dynamos and threw as great an increase of current over the system as the safety catches would I permit, at various times for about one second while this current was passing; the incandesence lamps would I give an unwonted glow, and every induction coil and' motor surreptitiously attached to the system would re- ceive an extra current designed to burn it. In this manner the system is occasionally cleared of all tres- passers.—Enyineering. ARCTIC EXPLORATIoN.—Captain Deuchars, of the Dundee whaler Jan Mayen, has received from Dr. Franz 130a5,1 Berlin, a copy of a. chart showing the explorations he made in the winter of 1883-4 of Cumberland Gulf. In I 1883 Dr. Boas sailed to the gulf in the whaler Germania, and twintered at the Bikerten Islands. During the; winter and spring Dr. Boas—who was accompanied by a Iservant and well provided with sledges, &c.—surveyed the north shore of the gulf as far as Cape Mercy, crossed to Niatlik, and travelled round the head of the gulf, making a thorough examination of the coast and the outlying islands. Having finished this survey of the gulf Dr. Boas left his headquarters in the summer of 1884, and journeyed to Cape Searle. He then skirted the west coast of Davis Straits, as far north as Cape Eater. In the autumn he returned south, and made 1 arrangements to winter with a tribe of Esquimaux at Cape Hooper; but :the Dundee whalers Jan Mayen and ; Nova Zembla came in sight, and the doctor went on ! board the former. Afterwards he was, at his own re- 1 quest, transferred to the American whaler- Wolff, as he wished to visit New York before returningro Germany.l The shores of Cumberland Gulf have hitherto been little ' known. During his explorations, Dr. Boas depended I mostly for his supplies of food on his rifle and on barter- ing with the natives, who treated him with the greatest !kindness. UNWHOLESOME HOUSES.—At a recent meeting of the National Health Society, presided over by Sir Robert Rawlinson, C. 8., a paper, written by Mrs. Priestley, was read on "Unseen Dangers in the Home," drawing atten- tion to some of the evils which lay unseen and unsus- pected ,under the very foundations of houses, and the dangers of damp in badly chosen sites. She pointed out that the best protection against all fermenting fevers was to sweep away one of the chief causes, by institut- ing a system of vigorous cleanliness in and round about the house, and also by living personally in accordance with the rules of health. It was urged that the house should be regarded not as a mere dead thing, consisting of inanimate walls and floors. You must treat your house as you would a faithful servant.. It would either be your friend or your enemy, according to the amount of consideration or neglect it received. Daily, care should be taken to wash and tend it., It was undesirable to obscure the light by covering the windows with too nu- merous folds of lace, blinds, and curtains. This was to choke the house by pressing on its windpipe. The win- dows must be opened wide and given an air bath every morning. The air was to be cleansed, if possible, as it entered. Care should be taken to drink clean water by having the cisterns and filters properly' and regularly cleansed. It was stated that disinfectants should never be used for pipes; they did no good, but endless mis- chief. Sunshine could be courted and welcome. It was nature's deodorise'', nature's best medicine, and for the spirits there was no better charm. The chairman said that the first necessity of house sanitation was to insure purity of atmosphere. This would not be done by leaving things to themselves, nor very likely by de- pending upon servants; it must be done by the mistress of the establishment He was sorry to say that a great many people had a strange prejudice to open air. He knew that some, during the frequent event of a London fog, would shut up every door and window in the house and endeavour to exclude every particle of air, hoping by this to escape the fog, although it was perfectly cer- tain that it would penetrate into any house in spite of closed doors and windows. In a modern building there should never be a drain within the four walls of the ; house; they should always be outside.

The Author of the above-mentioned work wishes to make a few remarks to persons who' may apprehend that they are in the early stages or in an advanced state of disease. He would press upon them the necessity of not postponing a step on which their whole future health and happiness may be at stake, but to at once apply for competent and trustworthy advice, on wbich they can fully rely. These observations are not made with any intention of extolling his own abilities, as lieus satisfied to let his reputation rest where it is, as he can fairly lay claim to having succeeded in restor- ing the blessings of health with all its glori- ous attributes to many who had been pro- nounced INCURABLE when they were in- duced to apply to him as a last chance, for them the most happy of chances. He therefore cannot close his eyes to these facts, that the remedies he use have cured when many others hao failed, nor do we mention it in disparage- ment of any of our Professional contempora- ries, but as plain unvarnished truths. It is a well known fact that many a e ruined through ignorance and wrong treatment. Front the daily observations or the author, be ears fully corroborate this. Myriads of broken-down, wretched invalids are constantly crowding upon his attention whose misery and wretchedness are owing wholly or in part to the ignorance of previous medical advisers, and he feels constrained to admonish invalids of this class to confide the treatment of their Cases to none except those who devote their whole energy and abilities to the treatment of nervous and special maladies, and who give undoubted evidence of their superior qualifica- tions and fitness for the same. LONDON, THURSDAY. Parliament will be occupied throughout the whole of next week in the ceremony of swearing-in members. The election of the Speaker, which in some circumstances might be counted upon to lead to an exciting debate and division, will be quietly accomplished, Mr. Peel being re-elected by the unanimous vote of the House. It is probable that Mr. Parnell will take the opportunity of expressing his dissent and that of his colleagues. The fact as Mr. Peel has been too much for the Parnellites. Sir Henry Brand dealt with them with what was at the time regarded as firmness, and at the close of his term of office received a tribute from Mr. Parnell, who formally dissociated himself and his colleagues from the vote of thanks which the House passed to the retiring Speaker. But Mr. Peel has far exceeded Sir Henry Bra'nd in the readiness - and resolution with which he has curbed obstruction. Had it suited the tactics of the Conservatives to carry out their original resolution and oppose the re-election of Mr. Peel, they would have had the hearty con- currence of the Parnellites. Since there is to be no division the Parnellites will have no other resource than to make a harmless demonstration. The swearing-in of a new Parliament is in ordi- nary times a very dull affair. The first member to take the oath and sign the Roll of Parliament is the Speaker, the next two signatures being those who proposed and seconded his election. Then the members for Bedfordshire sign, the custom being to take the constituencies in alphabetical order, beginning with the counties, at the head of which stands Bedfordshire. The clerk at the table is sup- posed to go right through the list both of boroughs and counties But as a matter of fact he does not get very far through the alphabet with the coun- ties, and when he ceases members are at liberty in- discriminately to sign. An hour or two of this is quite sufficient for the ordinary spectator. But the ceremony that will begin on Tuesday is likely to be spiced with excitement of the familiar kind pro- vided by Mr. Bradlaugh. That the member for Northampton means to take the oath is well known, but the precise method of his procedure he keeps a secret.

What will most probably happen will be that— presuming the ordinary course is taken—Mr. Brad- laugh will come up with the first group that make for the table after the clerk has ceased to recite the names in alphabetical order. Should he do so, there can be nothing to prevent his taking the oath and signing the roll with the rest. The House of Com- mons would not be fully constituted, and the mem- bers who have been sworn in could not take upon themselves the functions of a full House. It has been suggested that Sir Erskine-May might literally carry out the instruction which directs that mem- bers shall be sworn in in the alphabetical order of their constituences. In such case the great majority of the House would be sworn in before Northampton was reached. But it would be un- worthy of the House to play such a trick, and the Speaker may be counted upon to discountenance a suggestion which on other grounds is unworkable. It may be taken for granted that Mr. Bradlaugh will by hook or by crook get himself sworn in, and that as soon as possible thereafter the Conservatives and the Parnellites will combine to expel him. The tug of war will begin on Thursday week,. when the queen's Speech will be read and the policy of the Government disclosed. I hear from a source that has often proved reliable, that the inertia of the Cabinet has proved too much for Lord Randolph Churchill, and that his bold scheme of taking the Irish bull by the horns has been defeated. His pro- posal, which had the support of Lord Carnarvon, was to adopt Mr. Gladstone's policy set forth in the speech delivered by him upon his arrival in Edin- burgh in November. I quoted last week the sentence in which this policy is indicated. In effect, it de- clared that, short of tampering with the integrity of the Empire, Mr. Gladstone was willing to go any lengths in conceding local government to Ire- land. Lord Randolph's move was a clever one, and the arguments by which he supported it seemed convincing. The Irish difficulty must be settled sooner or later, and sooner better than later. The question was, who was to be the agent for carrying , out the good work, the Conservatives or • the Liberals? Lord Randolph desired to secure the, honour for his own party, and pointed out that Mr. Gladstone, bound by his spoken and recorded words, would be obliged to co-operate with thsra in.carry- ing such a scheme. But Lord Randolph argued to deaf ears. and it has been decided that all that will be offered will be a scheme of local government ap- plicable to the -United Kingdom. This, of course, will not be acceptable to the Irish members who will thus be driven into the arms of Mr. Gladstone. From him they will obtain a just and generous measure, but they will deceive themselves if they imagine they will get anything more. It would be incredible that they should harbour aspirations after more, were it not that one finds even among Liberals a curious suspicion that Mr. Gladstone is prepared to pay any price to secure the pacification of Ireland. Only yesterday the mem- ber for a large constituency in the midlands made quite a little speech to me showing how he had taken great pains to ascertain the drift of opinion amongst his constituents and found that it was "dead against separation!" As far as practical issues are concerned, he might as well have occu- pied his time in ascertaining their views on the comparative convenience of walking on their hands or legs. The question of separation is not before the country, and indeed never can be made a ques- tion. If there is one point upon which Radicals. Tories, Conservatives, Liberals, Whigs, and even the Independent members are united, it is the deter- mination to maintain the integrity of the empire. To talk as my friend did yesterday is to display an amount of ignorance of the actual situation, which is one of the greatest obstacles Mr. Gladstone will have to grapple with. The great event of the week in London—a point of interest outweighing the approaching meeting of Parliament— has been the snow storm. London went to bed on Tuesday night in its customary drear colours, and woke in the morning to find itself clothed in white. The suddenness of the changed appearance was equalled by the upsetting of all the arrangements of social life. The snow came clown in large soft fleeces that speedily made the white cloak four or five inches thick. When the snowstorm stopped the thaw set in, the roads became rivers of slush, vehicular traffic was almost suspended, and even at night, when a good deal of the snow had diappeared, it was almost impossible to get a cab, and when the cab was procured it was next to impossible to .get along. It was a great day of triumph for the underground railway, which in days of fog or snow drives a rattling business. The loss to busses and trams was more than pro- portionately great. Most of the hansoms drove tandem, the four wheelers also doubling their motive power. But no cabman would take a fare for a distance of two miles, and then expected double fare, which was indeed-his due. To-day it is freezing hard, with more snow threatening. On the 28th of May next there will happen a new episode in a famous drama, which in its time con- centrated upon the Court at Westminster the atten- tion of the civilised world. On that day Sir Henry Alfred Joseph Doughty-Tich borne comes of age, and will enter into the possessions that have accumu- lated during his long minority. The estate was deeply dipped into to meet the charges arising out of the case of the Claimant, but it is said that it has since been so carefully nursed that the new baronc;-, has come into a rent roll of nearly £30,000 a year. Arthur Orton claimed the property as the eldest son of the lost passenger in the Bella. The present baronet was many years younger. He was, indeed, a posthumus child, and was born right into the baronetcy, which is one of tee most ancient although not nearly so old as the family, who were great people in Hampshire before the conquest. Whilst the young heir thus comes into full enjoyment of his fortune, the man who claimed it is earning a precarious living at pigeon matches, whilst the woman who called herself' and was by many hailed as Lady Tichbome, is with her two children living in a workhouse.

A short time ago the World printed a piteous story about Louis Kossouth, describing him and his family as being in a state of destitution. Last week the World made frank acknowledgment of its error. The fact is that Kossouth is living at Turin in very comfortable circumstances. He made a good deal of money by the lectures he delivered in England, which, added to the money possessed by his wife, secured him a competency. His two sons are also doing well, one being manager of the South Eastern Railroad of Italy, and the other superinten- dent of sulphur mines. The great Hungarian pa- triot is reported to be in excellent health, cheerily bearing the burden of his 84 years.

Miss Kate Field, an American journalist for a long time resident in London, sends to a friend an ac- count of a funny adventure that has befallen her. She went to the Lyceum Theatre, New York, to see a performance called "One of our girls." She was so pleased with it that she wrote a note to the man-

ager expressing her high approval of the piece. 1 The#Aute manager had the note lithographed and sent it out in a sealed envelope to forty thousand of the principal people in New York and the neigh- bourhood. The transfer was so cleverly done that it was impossible, except upon close examination, to detect that the sheet was lithographed. The re- sult has been most embarrassing. Every morning brings to Miss Field hundreds of letters containing the note addressed to the theatrical manager and surmising that in the hurry of the moment Miss Field raix.ed up letters and envelopes and has sent to the theatrical manager the note intended for the 1 correspondent who returns the lithograph.

In one way, and that an unexpected way, this first week of the Millais Exhibition has been ex- traordinarily interesting. Fully a third of the painters' works now on view are portraits, and the portraits are, of course, chiefly of beautiful women and of titled, wealthy, or remarkable men. Men or women they were all anxious to see how their pic- tures took in the Bond-street Gallery. There is this about Millais, as a portrait painter, that he al- ways gets likenesses, and the result is that after staring at the canvasses on the walls you get quite a start to find that they have come down from their frames and are walking about the gallery. In the case of the ladies this is not so noticeable, as there is a greater variety of dress, and many of them are taken in evening dress. The men mostly go to the Grosvenor in similar or the same clothes that they wore at the studio, and so the effect is at once per- plexina and amusing. I need scarcely say that in- directly this is the greatest homage to the painter.
•,L,retttrs to the editor:
A STREET NUISANCE.

Sir,—Has Inspector Norman not yet returned from his Christmas holidays that the vile oleaginous odours emitted by peripatetic "chipped potatoe" boxes remain undetected? I am sure if the Inspector only once got a "sniff" of the pltato perfumes which nightly assail the olfactory nerves of pedestrians in our principal streets, a speedy stop would be put to what has at length become an uamitigated nuisance. Compared to the emissions of these travelling stewing ovens, the odours at Longford are delightful, and it lots been a matter of sur- prise to me that these vehicles have not been complained of before, and the nuisance suppressed. Trusting ere long to see this matter remedied, I am, dtc., J. G. R. Warrington, January 8, 1886.

div.head: PEACE SOCIETY.
div.p: THE PEACE SOCIETY.

Sir,—Nothing but a strict sense of duty prompts me to notice the letter of your correspondent" Hodge," which ap- peared in your issue of December 12th, for I have a positive repugnance to entering on a newspaper controversy with one who shields himself from responsibility behind a nom de plume, especially when he is attacking a position already taken up. It hurts not me to be told that, in advocating the principles of the Peace t- ociety, lam a faddist. I console inysof for this with the fact that I am in good company. He tries to fasten on the Peace Society the charge that war .by the Tories we strongly condemn, whilst war by the Liberals we meekly condone, and indulges in a bit of high falutin that is worthy of the late Lord Beaconsfield himself, for he says :—" The particular fad of which Mr. eathaone is the exponent is clearly that which finds embodiment in toe Peace Society, a society which, without doubt, has done more to bring down unmerited scorn and obloquy on peace dectrines than any other agency in the three kingdoms." I am 'glad he admits the scorn is unmerited, but I apprehend it is born of disappointment at the rapid spread of those doctrines in those who are opposed to them and whose in- terest it is to frustrate them. Then he tells us " that the society is a combination of party politicians, whose special function seems to be to find distinctions where none exist, for party purposes ;" and asks, " who does not remember the sudden access of piety and humanitarianism amongst the members of the Peace Society when the Tories were in office and engaged in war." " But when Alexandria was bombarded, when Egyptians were slaugh- tered like sheep, and naked Arabs were shot down in thou- sands with arms of precision, why then of course it was a different thing." Dear me! what a terrible indictment this would be—if there were only a shadow of truth in it. But what a base calumny on a society actuated by the noblest' and most exalted motives, to philanthropic principles, and how absurd and ridiculous when it is found to have no foundation in fact! For who but "lodge" does not re- member that this Egyptian policy has been opposed and proteFted against by the Peace Society at every stage in its progress? Who, but Hodge, does not know that this , one question has done more than all others to set the mem- bers of the Peace Society, and the rest of the Liberal party by the ears ? Who, but " Hodge," has not read of the members of the Peace Society in the House of Commons making common cause with the Tories, though with an honester purpose, both by vote and speech strongly con- demning the late Government for its meddling policy? and who, but" Hodge," has not heard this policy assailed outside, both at public meetings, lectures, and in petitions, at the instance of the Peace Society? Having said this much, I am free to ask Hodge who made him a ruler and a judge over us? Or, if be has any voice in the councils of that party whose cause he so ably cham- pions, what hope have we of assistance from them in the future ? or what encouragement have we received in the past? If the members of the Peace Society and the Tory party in Parliament have united in protestifig against the Liberal policy their actions have sprung from diametrically Gpposite motives; for whilst the action of the Peace party has been due to consistent opposition to that which they be- lieved to be morally wrong the action of the Tory party has been because the Government has not gone far enough, and they have done their utmost to egg them on and push them further and further into the policy of aggression and war. Which party was it that cheered loudest when the bombardment of Alexandria was announced in Parliament, or when the news came of the battle of Tel-el-Kebir ? Was any protest raised against these measures by the Tory party then? No! Then why this sudden "access of piety and humanitarianism" now; why this simulated indigna- tion at the slaughter of Egyptians, and this hypocritical display of sympathy for the naked Arabs? Everybody but " Hodge," perhaps, knows why it is. Therefore, let the charge of inconsistency recoil back on his own party. At least, let them wait till their own hands are clean, before presuming to be self-constituted judges of others. There is another matter, in which " lodge's" affected Ignorance over-reaches itself, when he asks "Does he mean to insinuate that Lord Salisbury, the Prime Minister of the British Empire, and one of the ablest and most illustrious of Englishmen, is an inveterate liar?" I answer that neither his abilite, his illustrious name, nor his exalted position in the State are sufficient to blot out of remem- brance, the unfortunate record of his public prevaricating utterances, and if "lodge ' again does not know what everyone else does know, I will inform him that his great illustrious "Name, to every eve the climax of all scorn, stands on high" as the contemptuous- synonym fpr false- , hood.

The society of which' Hedge" speaks so contemptuously bas become a great and recognised power in the country, whose ramifications are spreading wider mid wider, whose influence, despite the splenetic and vapid utterances of " Hodge " and his compatriots, is becoming more and more manifest in the councils of nations year by year, and whose work in the cause of humanity if slow, is sure, and must in the end prevail, inasmuch as their priaciples are based, not on mere selfishness and expediency, but on equity, jus- tice, and common sense.—l am, yours, &c., A. RATHBONE. 43, Arpiey-street, Warrington.

div.head: CHURCH INFLUENCE.
div.p: CHURCH INFLUENCE.

Sir,—You will, perhaps, kindly insert a few words from me on the great and all important subject of Church in- fluence. Its importance arises from the fact that we have seen and felt during the recent elections such a series of manceuvres as, if not at once put a step to, are likely to debase and degrade a large portion of the population. It may be said that this is a mere question of opinion. In answer to this, I say proof in abundance teems in the daily press, and if more were wanted it. was to be found in the fact that circulars were issued, alike by Churchmen and brewers, calling upon the people to support Tories. The brewers' influence is great only amongst the residuum, the class w;io, passing the beat part of their lives in the tap-room, are content to act as the tools of a body of men who are sub- ject to and controlled by a most stringent and unpatriotic trade union.

• The influence of the Church is felt by another and very different class of men. The Church is essentially the home of the aristocrat; as such it is looked uo to with a reverence, not at all surprising, by those who hope to gather the crumbs that fall from the rich man's table. The question is, " Have the people a right to expect the influence of the Church to be on their side, and if it is en their side, how is it to make itself felt? " Can anyone doubt that if the Church had been as anxious to place the agricultural labourer on a sound and honourable footing in his native village as it has been to seek alliance with the squire and insist upon its tithes but what the peasant to- day would have been the mainstay of the Established Church. Church dignitaries are now crying aloud for reform. Those acquaietted with Church history do not need to he told that this cry is not of modern growth. In 1E36 the Ecclesi-stical Commissioners were entrusted with the task of reforming the Church. How did they do their work? In half-a-dozen parishes they augmented the livings by diviclng £4B amongst the clergy. On six bishop's palaces they expended the sum of £134,310. Yet in these very dioceses there were :- 502 livings under £lOO a year each 85 do. do. 50 do. dn. 68 do. do. 40 do. do. 10 do. do. 30 do. do. 8 do. do. 20 do. do. 1 do. do. 10 do. do. The Commissioners thought more of the bloated bishop than of the poor parson. I ask was the influence of those in tomer in favour of the people? Decidedly not. The policy adopted has been to enrich the few, so as to keep preferments worth having open to the aristocratic younger sons. The poor curate, who, in nine cases out of ten, had to do the parish work, must be kept like those he was told uff to visit the poor. Has the church educated the poor? In 1781 a Dissent- Lig minister at Gloucester, aided by Robert Raikes, the printer, started the first Sunday school, and it was not till

FST NEWS.
SUPPOSED WRECK OF A PASSENGER STEAMER.

Little doubt is now entertained but that a passenger steamer has gone down in the Channel. No trace of the vessel's name has yet been found. A cabin door indicative of a baker's room was wasked ashore at Jersey on Friday, as well as a board, on which was painted " No smoking allowed in this cabin." A bunk has also been picked up the bottom of which is of galvanized ,heop iron.

SURVEYOR'S REPORT.—Mr. Owen reported, with regard to Lodge-lane' Bewsey, that he had, as requested, inspected the foul ditch, and had to report that to carry a sewer from the hoivf in the lane to Sankey brook would cost about £4O, but if a short cut acrosa a neck of land was allowed by the landowner whose land the houses stand upon which create the nuisance, the cost would be about £3O. Mr. Thomas Dambill, Greystone Heath, Penketh, having ap- plied for permission to remove a pail closet from the south to the north side of his yard at Penketh, he had granted the necessary permit on their behalf. Mr. John Jackson, Grevstone Heath, Penketh, submitted plans for a new stable and coach-house to his house at Penketh, and alst; plans for eight houses to be erected on land adjoining his house. The plans were in accordance with the bye-laws, and might be accepted. The Hon. Leopold W. H. !ANNUAL BALL AT NEWTON —The annual ball in connection with thetNewton Football Club took place in the Town Hall. Newton, on New Year's night. There were a good number of people present, and dancing was indulged in with much spirit to the strains of Stirrup's band until about five o'clock on Saturday morning. The refreshments were supplied by Mr. Walmalev, of the Legh Arms. PRINITIEE METHODUT SCHOLARS' TREAT.—The elder portion ef the scholars attending the Primitive Methodist Sunday School, Lord-street, Earlestown were entertained to a very enjoyable tea in that schoolroom on New Year's Day. The juveniles had been similarly treated on the day following Christmas Day, and the second gathering was reserved for the adult scholars. About 130 partook of an excellent tea, which was served by lady friends, including Miss Worsley, Miss Wood, Miss Jackson, Mrs. Arrowsmith, and a number of the senior scholars. After the tables had been cleared away the company spent the evening in var- ious games appropriate to the season. The proceedings throughout were of a very enjoyable character. The ar- rangements were satisfactorily carried out under the direc- tions of Mr. J. Woods (superintendent) and Mr. W. Banton (secretary.)

As the death- rate of this country is very high. considering its sanitary arrangements, a large amount of money is expended annually in the purchase of MOURNING, thus calling into existence a num- ber of shops exclusively for the Sale of Mourning Goods. At these establishments it has been the practice to charge enormous prices for very in- ferior class articles. A sudden death in a family, mourning has to be purchased quickly. The &Fib place that suggests itself is a mourning shop we have seen or beard about.
